description: Chemistry from high-school foundations to master's-level understanding, rooted in everyday life and practice: atoms and the periodic table, bonding, states of matter and solutions, thermochemistry and equilibrium, acids/bases and electrochemistry, kinetics and catalysis, organic structure, synthesis and spectroscopy, inorganic and materials chemistry, quantum and computational chemistry, biochemistry and polymers, analytical, environmental and industrial chemistry.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is a mole, and why do chemists need it?
notes.back: A fixed count, \(6.022\times10^{23}\) entities. It converts between grams you can weigh and atoms you can't count.
notes.analogy: Like a 'dozen' for atoms: a counting unit big enough that a mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 g.
notes.extra: In practice: molar mass in g/mol is the exchange rate between the scale and the reaction.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why is stoichiometry best seen as bookkeeping?
notes.back: Atoms are conserved, so a balanced equation is a ledger: every atom debited on the left must be credited on the right, in mole ratios.
notes.analogy: Double-entry accounting: the equation balances or you've lost money (atoms).
notes.extra: Pitfall: ratios are in moles, never in grams.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is the limiting reagent, and how do you find it?
notes.back: The reactant that runs out first. Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest quotient is limiting and sets the maximum product.
notes.analogy: Making sandwiches: 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese. Cheese limits you, however much bread you have.
notes.extra: In practice: cheap reagents are used in excess so the expensive one is fully consumed.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why is a percent yield below 100% normal, and what can it never exceed?
notes.back: Side reactions, incomplete equilibrium and losses on purification reduce it. Above 100% means the product is wet or impure.
notes.analogy: A pipeline's throughput after retries and drops: never more than what went in.
notes.extra: Formula: actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why are significant figures a matter of honesty?
notes.back: They state how precisely you know a number. Writing 12.3456 from a 12.3 g balance claims precision your instrument never had.
notes.analogy: Quoting a latency as 12.3456 ms from a clock that ticks in 0.1 ms is false precision in the report.
notes.extra: Rule: multiply/divide keeps the fewest sig figs; add/subtract keeps the fewest decimal places.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is effective nuclear charge (\(Z_{eff}\)) and why does it matter?
notes.back: The net pull an outer electron feels: \(Z_{eff} = Z - S\), nuclear charge minus shielding by inner electrons. It drives nearly every periodic trend.
notes.analogy: A concert from the back row: the stage (nucleus) is loud, but the crowd in front (inner electrons) muffles it.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why does an inner-shell electron shield much better than another electron in the same shell?
notes.back: Inner electrons sit between nucleus and outer electron, cancelling charge. Same-shell electrons are at similar distance and shield only about 35%.
notes.extra: Slater: same-shell electrons contribute 0.35, the n−1 shell 0.85, deeper shells 1.00 each.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Across a period, why does atomic radius shrink?
notes.back: Each step adds a proton, but the new electron enters the same shell and shields poorly, so \(Z_{eff}\) rises and pulls the cloud in.
notes.extra: Down a group: a new shell is added, so radius grows.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why does ionisation energy rise across a period and fall down a group?
notes.back: Across: higher \(Z_{eff}\), smaller radius, tighter hold. Down: the outer electron is farther away and shielded, so it leaves easily.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than nitrogen?
notes.back: Oxygen's 4th 2p electron is paired in an orbital, and pair repulsion makes it easier to remove. Nitrogen's half-filled 2p³ is stable.
notes.analogy: Two people sharing a seat are more eager to leave than one alone in each seat.
notes.extra: Same dip: Be to B, from the 2p electron being higher than the full 2s.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is electronegativity, and why does fluorine top the scale?
notes.back: A bonded atom's tendency to pull shared electrons. Fluorine is small with high \(Z_{eff}\), so bonding electrons sit very close to its nucleus.
notes.analogy: A tug-of-war where fluorine is the heaviest, closest anchor.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Electronegativity vs electron affinity: how do they differ?
notes.back: Electron affinity: energy released adding an electron to an isolated gas atom. Electronegativity: pull on electrons within a bond, a scale not a measurement.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.text: Chlorine, not fluorine, has the most exothermic electron affinity, because fluorine is so {{c1::small}} that added electrons {{c2::repel strongly}} in its compact 2p shell.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why are the noble gases inert?
notes.back: Full outer shells mean no unpaired electrons, a very high ionisation energy, and near-zero electron affinity. There is nothing to gain from bonding.
notes.analogy: A fully booked server: no capacity left to accept or give anything.
notes.extra: Exception: heavy Xe (low enough IE) forms XeF₂, XeF₄ with fluorine.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why does sodium react violently with water but lithium merely fizzes?
notes.back: Sodium melts from the reaction heat, exposing fresh metal and accelerating. Lithium's higher melting point and slower kinetics keep it from running away.
notes.extra: Surprise: Li has the most negative \(E^\circ\), so thermodynamics isn't the reason; kinetics and melting point explain the fizz.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.text: Chromium is [Ar]{{c1::3d⁵4s¹}}, not 3d⁴4s², and copper is [Ar]{{c2::3d¹⁰4s¹}}: half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable.
notes.extra: Why: 3d and 4s are close in energy, and exchange energy favours parallel spins.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What are isotopes, and why do they behave almost identically in chemistry?
notes.back: Same proton count, different neutrons. Chemistry depends on electrons, so only mass-dependent rates and physical properties change.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: How does carbon-14 dating work?
notes.back: Living things replenish ¹⁴C from air; at death intake stops and ¹⁴C decays (half-life ~5,730 y). The remaining ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio gives the age.
notes.analogy: A sealed battery's charge: you read the time since it was last topped up.
notes.extra: Limit: reaches ~50,000 years.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why does heavy water (D₂O) slow chemistry and biology?
notes.back: Deuterium doubles hydrogen's mass, so C–D and O–D bonds have lower zero-point energy and are harder to break (kinetic isotope effect).
notes.extra: In practice: D₂O moderates neutrons in reactors and is toxic to cells in large fractions.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: How is isotope labelling used to prove a reaction mechanism?
notes.back: Swap one atom for a heavy isotope (¹⁸O, D, ¹³C) and see where it ends up. In ester hydrolysis, ¹⁸O in the product shows which bond broke.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why must natural uranium be enriched for most reactors?
notes.back: Natural U is 99.3% ²³⁸U, which doesn't sustain a chain reaction; ²³⁵U (0.7%) does. Chemically identical, so separation uses tiny mass differences.
notes.extra: How: UF₆ gas through centrifuges; the lighter ²³⁵UF₆ gathers near the axis.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: Why is gold yellow while silver is white?
notes.back: Heavy nuclei speed inner electrons to a notable fraction of c, contracting s orbitals and expanding d, so blue light (~2.4 eV) is absorbed.
notes.extra: Also: mercury is liquid because its relativistically contracted 6s pair binds weakly to neighbours.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is the lanthanide contraction, and what practical result does it have?
notes.back: 4f electrons shield poorly, so radius shrinks steadily across the lanthanides. Hence Zr and Hf (and Nb/Ta) are near-identical in size and hard to separate.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: What is the diagonal relationship, with an example?
notes.back: Diagonal neighbours (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) are alike because charge density balances: higher charge rises with smaller size. Both Li and Mg form nitrides.

notes.deck: Chemistry::01 Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
notes.front: How does Slater's rule estimate \(Z_{eff}\) for a 2p electron in oxygen?
notes.back: \(S = 5\times0.35 + 2\times0.85 = 3.45\), so \(Z_{eff} = 8 - 3.45 = 4.55\). Same-shell electrons count 0.35 each; the 1s pair counts 0.85 each.
notes.extra: Limit: crude; computed \(Z_{eff}\) from self-consistent field (SCF) methods is more accurate.

notes.front: Why is bonding a continuum from ionic to covalent to metallic?
notes.back: Bond type depends on electronegativity difference and size. Large gap: ionic; similar and high: covalent; similar and low: metallic. Most bonds are mixed.
notes.analogy: A dimmer, not a switch: electron sharing slides smoothly from 'one owns it' to 'both own it'.

notes.front: Why does salt dissolve in water as ions while sugar dissolves as intact molecules?
notes.back: Water's dipoles solvate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ strongly enough to pay the lattice cost. Sugar's –OH groups hydrogen-bond to water, so its molecules separate whole.
notes.extra: In practice: salt solution conducts; sugar solution doesn't.

notes.front: Why does table salt form cubes?
notes.back: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ alternate in a simple cubic lattice, each ion surrounded by six opposite neighbours. Crystal faces mirror the internal packing.
notes.analogy: Stacking identical boxes: the macro shape reflects the repeat unit.

notes.front: What is lattice energy, and what makes it larger?
notes.back: Energy released forming a solid lattice from gaseous ions. It rises with ion charge and falls with ion size: ∝ \(q_+q_-/r\).
notes.extra: Example: MgO (2+/2−) has far higher lattice energy than NaCl, hence a melting point near 2800 °C.

notes.front: What does the Born–Haber cycle do?
notes.back: Applies Hess's law to a salt's formation: sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron affinity and lattice energy sum to the enthalpy of formation, letting you find the lattice term.
notes.analogy: Reconciling a ledger by two routes between the same start and end.

notes.front: What is the octet rule, and why does it work for period 2?
notes.back: Atoms tend to share/transfer electrons to reach 8 valence electrons: one s and three p orbitals are the only valence ones available there.

notes.front: Name the three kinds of octet-rule failure with an example each.
notes.back: Electron-deficient: BF₃. Odd-electron: NO. Expanded octet: SF₆.

notes.front: What is formal charge, and how do you use it to choose between Lewis structures?
notes.back: \(FC = V - N_{nonbonding} - \tfrac{1}{2}N_{bonding}\). Prefer structures with charges near zero and negatives on the more electronegative atoms.
notes.analogy: A bookkeeping assumption of equal sharing, not a real charge.

notes.front: What is resonance, and is the molecule flipping between structures?
notes.back: No. Real structure is a single hybrid of several Lewis forms; electrons are delocalised, giving bond lengths in between and extra stability.
notes.analogy: A mule is a blend of horse and donkey, not a creature flipping between them.
notes.extra: Examples: benzene, carboxylate, ozone.

notes.front: What experimental fact shows benzene is not alternating single and double bonds?
notes.back: All six C–C bonds are the same length (140 pm), between single (154) and double (134). It's also more stable than cyclohexatriene predicted.

notes.front: What is the logic of VSEPR?
notes.back: Regions of electron density repel, so they take positions as far apart as possible. Lone pairs take more room than bonding pairs.
notes.analogy: Balloons tied together at a point: they spread out to avoid each other.
notes.extra: Name: valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory.

notes.front: Why is water bent, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Two bonds plus two lone pairs give a tetrahedral arrangement (104.5°), so the O–H dipoles don't cancel. Polar water dissolves salts and hydrogen-bonds.
notes.extra: Contrast: linear CO₂ has polar bonds but no net dipole.

notes.front: What is hybridisation good for in organic chemistry?
notes.back: It explains shapes: sp³ gives 109.5°, sp² 120° with a π bond, sp 180° with two π bonds. It is a bookkeeping model for geometry.
notes.extra: Limit: H₂S bonds near 92°, so little hybridisation occurs there.

notes.front: Sigma vs pi bonds: how do they differ?
notes.back: Sigma: head-on overlap, symmetric about the bond axis, can rotate. Pi: sideways p overlap above and below the axis, weaker, and blocks rotation.
notes.extra: Consequence: cis/trans isomers exist because C=C won't rotate.

notes.text: Bond order up means bond length {{c1::down}} and bond strength {{c2::up}}: C–C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm, C≡C {{c3::120 pm}}.

notes.front: What does molecular orbital theory say that Lewis structures can't?
notes.back: Atomic orbitals combine into delocalised bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals; electrons fill them. It predicts magnetism and bond order.
notes.analogy: Two sine waves adding in phase (bonding) or cancelling (antibonding).

notes.front: Why doesn't He₂ exist?
notes.back: Two 1s orbitals make σ and σ*. Four electrons fill both, bond order \((2-2)/2=0\): antibonding cancels bonding.

notes.front: Why is O₂ paramagnetic, which Lewis theory can't explain?
notes.back: In the molecular orbital (MO) diagram the last two electrons enter the degenerate π* orbitals singly (Hund), leaving two unpaired spins and bond order 2.
notes.extra: Proof: liquid oxygen sticks to a strong magnet.

notes.front: Why is carbon monoxide deadly?
notes.back: CO binds the iron of haemoglobin ~200× more strongly than O₂. It is a strong σ-donor and π-acceptor, so oxygen can't be carried.
notes.analogy: Someone parking in your reserved space and never leaving.
notes.extra: Also: bound CO makes haemoglobin hold its remaining O₂ more tightly, so tissues get even less.

notes.front: Why does ice float?
notes.back: Hydrogen bonds lock water into an open hexagonal lattice that is ~9% less dense than the liquid, where molecules pack closer.
notes.extra: Why it matters: lakes freeze from the top, insulating life below.

notes.front: Why do oil and water separate?
notes.back: Water prefers hydrogen bonding with itself. Non-polar oil can't join in, and placing it breaks water's bonds: entropy favours unmixing.
notes.extra: In practice: soap molecules bridge both phases.

notes.front: What is London dispersion force and why do noble gases liquefy?
notes.back: Temporary, induced dipoles from electron fluctuations attract neighbours. Bigger, more polarisable atoms attract more, so Xe boils far above He.
notes.analogy: A flicker in one atom nudges the next, like a Mexican wave of tiny dipoles.
notes.extra: Gecko feet: millions of setae stick by dispersion alone.

notes.front: How does band theory separate metals, semiconductors and insulators?
notes.back: Orbitals merge into bands. Metals: partly filled band. Insulators: full valence band, large gap. Semiconductors: small gap (~1 eV).
notes.extra: LEDs: the band gap sets the colour; a wider gap emits bluer light.

notes.front: Why is diamond hard but graphite slippery?
notes.back: Diamond: every C is sp³ in a rigid 3D covalent network. Graphite: sp² sheets with strong bonds inside but weak dispersion between layers.
notes.analogy: Diamond is a brick wall; graphite is a stack of paper.
notes.extra: Bonus: graphite conducts through delocalised π electrons.

notes.front: Why is the hypervalency debate relevant to SF₆, and what is Bent's rule?
notes.back: Modern calculations show d orbitals play little role; bonding is 3-centre-4-electron polar. Bent's rule: lone pairs and electropositive groups prefer hybrids rich in s character.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why can a diver on air get oxygen poisoning or nitrogen narcosis at depth, even though the air mix is unchanged?
notes.back: Each gas acts by its partial pressure \(P_i = x_i P_{total}\). At 40 m (5 atm) air's O₂ is ~1 atm and N₂ ~4 atm: same mix, far higher doses.
notes.extra: In practice: deep divers swap in helium (heliox/trimix) to cut the N₂ and O₂ partial pressures.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why do divers get the bends if they ascend too fast?
notes.back: At depth, extra N₂ dissolves in blood and tissue (Henry's law). Fast ascent drops pressure suddenly and the N₂ comes out as bubbles.
notes.analogy: Opening a shaken soda bottle: the dissolved gas had no time to leave quietly, so it forms bubbles inside.
notes.extra: Fix: slow ascent with decompression stops lets N₂ leave through the lungs.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: In the van der Waals equation \((P+\tfrac{an^2}{V^2})(V-nb)=nRT\), what do a and b correct for?
notes.back: a: attraction between molecules (lowers pressure). b: the volume molecules themselves occupy (less free space).
notes.analogy: An ideal gas is a ballroom of ghosts; a real gas has people who bump into each other (b) and cling to friends (a).
notes.extra: When it matters: high pressure and low temperature, near condensation.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why is propane sold as a liquid in a cylinder but methane (natural gas) is not?
notes.back: Propane's critical temperature (97 °C) is above room temperature, so pressure alone (~8 atm) liquefies it. Methane's (−82 °C) is far below, so no pressure can.
notes.extra: Why it's useful: a litre of liquid propane expands to ~270 L of gas, a compact energy store.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does the solid–liquid line in water's phase diagram slope backwards?
notes.back: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so pressure favours the denser liquid and lowers the melting point. Most substances slope forward.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the effect is tiny (~0.0075 °C per atm); ice skates glide mainly thanks to friction and surface premelting.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does dry ice turn straight to gas instead of melting at room pressure?
notes.back: CO₂'s triple point is at 5.1 atm. At 1 atm liquid CO₂ cannot exist, so solid sublimes at −78.5 °C.
notes.extra: In practice: dry ice cools without leaving a puddle. In a sealed bottle, the pressure builds dangerously.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why is supercritical CO₂ used to decaffeinate coffee?
notes.back: It dissolves caffeine like a liquid, penetrates beans like a gas, and its density (hence solvating power) is tunable by pressure. It leaves no solvent residue when depressurised.
notes.extra: Numbers: critical point of CO₂ is 31 °C and 73 atm, mild enough to spare the flavour.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker?
notes.back: The sealed pot raises pressure to ~2 atm, so water boils at ~120 °C instead of 100 °C. Rates roughly double per 10 °C rise.
notes.extra: Converse: on a mountain, lower pressure means water boils below 100 °C (~71 °C on Everest) and pasta takes longer.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: What does the Clausius–Clapeyron equation \(\ln P = -\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{RT}+C\) tell you?
notes.back: Vapour pressure rises exponentially with temperature. A plot of ln P against 1/T is a straight line of slope \(-\Delta H_{vap}/R\).
notes.extra: Use: predict boiling point at any pressure from two measured points.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does water form beads and a skin that supports a water strider?
notes.back: Surface molecules have neighbours only on one side, so they are pulled inward. The surface acts like a stretched film that minimises its area.
notes.analogy: A crowd at the edge of a square leans inward since nobody is outside to hold hands with.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does soap make water wet fabric better?
notes.back: Soap's amphiphilic molecules sit at the surface and cut surface tension, so water spreads into fibres instead of beading. Their hydrophobic tails also grab grease.
notes.extra: Contrast: surface tension of water ~72 mN/m falls to ~30 with detergent.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: What decides whether a liquid climbs a narrow tube (water in a paper towel) or is pushed down (mercury)?
notes.back: Adhesion to the walls versus cohesion within the liquid. Adhesion wins for water on glass (concave meniscus, rise); cohesion wins for mercury (convex, depression).
notes.extra: Examples: trees pulling water upward, paper towels, wicks.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Is glass a very slow-flowing liquid? Why do old windows look thicker at the bottom?
notes.back: No. Glass is an amorphous solid frozen below its glass transition; at room temperature it would take far longer than the universe's age to flow. Uneven old panes came from manufacturing.
notes.analogy: Like a traffic jam so tightly packed that no car moves in practice, though it has no tidy lanes.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why can a new polymorph wreck a drug, as with ritonavir (Norvir)?
notes.back: The same molecule can crystallise in different packings with different solubility. A more stable, less soluble form appeared unexpectedly, so capsules dissolved poorly and had to be reformulated.
notes.analogy: Same Lego bricks, a more compact build that's harder to take apart.
notes.extra: Rule: the most stable polymorph is least soluble; once its seed exists, it spreads everywhere.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does like dissolve like? Why don't oil and water mix?
notes.back: Dissolving needs solute–solvent attractions comparable to those lost. Water's hydrogen bonds hold on to each other and exclude nonpolar oil, which can only offer weak dispersion forces.
notes.analogy: Cliques at a party: polar guests mingle with polar guests; oil molecules have nothing to say to the water crowd.
notes.extra: Example: vitamin C (many –OH) is water-soluble; vitamin A (long hydrocarbon) is fat-soluble, so it accumulates in the body.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: What are the two energy terms behind \(\Delta H_{soln}\) of an ionic solid?
notes.back: Positive: breaking the lattice (lattice enthalpy). Negative: hydrating the ions. The sum can be either sign; entropy of mixing often makes dissolving favourable regardless.
notes.extra: Example: NaOH heats water (strongly hydrated); NH₄NO₃ cools it.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does most solid dissolve better when hot but gases dissolve worse?
notes.back: Dissolving most solids absorbs heat, so heating favours it (Le Chatelier). Dissolving a gas releases heat, so warmth drives it out.
notes.extra: In practice: warm soda goes flat; warm lakes hold less O₂ for fish.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does a soda fizz when opened? State Henry's law.
notes.back: \(C = k_H P\): dissolved gas concentration is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. Opening drops the CO₂ pressure and the excess escapes.
notes.extra: Pitfall: bubbles need nucleation sites: scratches, Mentos or dust.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Colligative properties depend on {{c1::the number of dissolved particles}}, not {{c2::their identity}}.
notes.text: Colligative properties depend on {{c1::the number of dissolved particles}}, not {{c2::their identity}}.
notes.extra: The four: vapour pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does salt on icy roads and antifreeze in a radiator work?
notes.back: \(\Delta T_f = i K_f m\). Solute dilutes the liquid, lowering its tendency to freeze, so ice melts or forms only at a lower temperature.
notes.extra: Choose: CaCl₂ (i≈3) beats NaCl (i≈2) per mole and works lower. NaCl's eutectic is −21 °C.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why does reverse osmosis purify seawater, and why do cells burst in pure water?
notes.back: Osmosis moves water toward higher solute concentration (\(\Pi = iMRT\)). RO applies pressure above seawater's ~27 atm to push water backwards through a membrane; a cell in pure water swells.
notes.analogy: Water flows to the busy bank, like users migrating to the more crowded server until pressure pushes back.
notes.extra: Contrast: salting meat or pickling dries microbes out by osmosis.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: How do a solution, colloid and suspension differ, and how does the Tyndall effect tell them apart?
notes.back: Particle size: <1 nm, 1 nm–1 µm, >1 µm. Colloids scatter a light beam visibly (Tyndall); solutions don't; suspensions settle.
notes.extra: Examples: sunbeams in fog, headlights in mist, milk's cloudiness.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: How does mayonnaise stay a stable oil-in-water emulsion?
notes.back: Egg-yolk lecithin and proteins are emulsifiers: they coat oil droplets, water-loving on one end, oil-loving on the other, preventing coalescence.
notes.analogy: Bouncers standing between oil droplets so they never merge.
notes.extra: Other types: milk (fat in water), fog (liquid in gas), butter (water in fat).

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: How do hand warmers (sodium acetate) and rock candy both exploit supersaturation?
notes.back: A solution holds more solute than equilibrium allows until a nucleus appears. Clicking the disc (or a string seed) triggers crystallisation; hand warmers release heat of fusion.
notes.analogy: Like a queue frozen at a one-way door until someone pushes through, then everyone follows.
notes.extra: Pitfall: clean, undisturbed solution means no nuclei, so it stays metastable.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: What does Raoult's law \(P_A = x_A P_A^*\) assume, and what happens if it fails?
notes.back: Ideal behaviour: A–B forces equal A–A and B–B forces. Stronger A–B attraction gives negative deviation, weaker gives positive.
notes.extra: In practice: sets vapour composition for distillation.

notes.deck: Chemistry::03 States of Matter, Solutions & Mixtures
notes.front: Why can't you distil ethanol past 95.6%?
notes.back: Ethanol–water shows positive deviation from Raoult's law and forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope (78.2 °C). Vapour and liquid have the same composition there, so distillation stalls.
notes.analogy: A load balancer that sends traffic in exactly the same ratio it received, so the split never improves.
notes.extra: Escape: molecular sieves, an entrainer such as benzene or cyclohexane, or pressure-swing distillation.

notes.front: How do enthalpy and internal energy differ?
notes.back: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V\). ΔH is the heat at constant pressure (open beaker); ΔU includes the work done pushing against the atmosphere.
notes.extra: For gases: \(\Delta H \approx \Delta U + \Delta n_{gas}RT\).

notes.front: How do an instant cold pack and a disposable hand warmer differ chemically?
notes.back: Cold pack: NH₄NO₃ dissolves endothermically (ΔH > 0). Hand warmer: iron oxidises exothermically (ΔH < 0) to Fe₂O₃, with salt and carbon speeding the rate.
notes.extra: Sign convention: ΔH < 0 means heat leaves the system to the surroundings.

notes.front: Why does Hess's law work?
notes.back: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on start and end, not the route. Add known steps to get one that can't be measured directly.
notes.analogy: Total elevation gain between two towns doesn't depend on the road you drive.
notes.extra: Use: \(\Delta H^\circ = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants})\); elements in their standard states are 0.

notes.front: Why does burning a fuel release energy? Is it energy 'stored in the bonds'?
notes.back: Not stored. Breaking bonds always costs energy; the products' C=O and O–H bonds are much stronger than the fuel's C–H and O=O bonds broken, so net energy is released.
notes.analogy: Like trading a cheap flimsy lock for an expensive strong one; the difference is paid out.
notes.extra: Numbers (kJ/mol): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O (in CO₂) ~800, O–H 464.

notes.front: Why do nitrogen-rich explosives release so much energy?
notes.back: They form N₂, whose N≡N triple bond (945 kJ/mol) is one of the strongest bonds, so the products are very stable compared with weak N–N or N–O bonds in the explosive.
notes.extra: Examples: trinitrotoluene (TNT), nitroglycerin, airbags (NaN₃ → N₂).

notes.front: Coffee-cup vs bomb calorimeter: what does each measure?
notes.back: Coffee-cup (constant pressure) gives \(\Delta H\) using \(q = mc\Delta T\). A sealed steel bomb (constant volume) gives \(\Delta U\).
notes.extra: Pitfall: remember the calorimeter itself absorbs heat; calibrate its heat capacity.

notes.front: How are food Calories defined, and why does fat give more than carbohydrate?
notes.back: 1 Calorie = 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Fat ~9 kcal/g, carbs and protein ~4, because fat's C–H-rich chains are less oxidised (hold less oxygen) and release more on full oxidation.
notes.extra: Ethanol: ~7 kcal/g.

notes.front: Which changes usually raise entropy in a reaction?
notes.back: Producing gas, increasing the number of particles, dissolving a solid, melting, heating. Look for more moles of gas on the product side.
notes.extra: Quick test: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂(g) has ΔS > 0 because gas appears.

notes.front: NH₄NO₃ dissolving is endothermic yet spontaneous. Why?
notes.back: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\). ΔH is +26 kJ/mol but the ions disperse in water so ΔS is large; \(T\Delta S\) outweighs ΔH.
notes.analogy: A cash-negative move that wins because it buys a lot of freedom (options).
notes.extra: Result: the solution cools as it draws heat from the surroundings.

notes.front: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\): ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 is {{c1::always spontaneous}}; ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 is {{c2::never spontaneous}}.
notes.text: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\): ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 is {{c1::always spontaneous}}; ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 is {{c2::never spontaneous}}.
notes.analogy: Enthalpy is the incentive, entropy is the freedom, and temperature sets how much freedom is worth.
notes.extra: Mixed cases: ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 favoured at low T (freezing); ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 favoured at high T (melting, boiling).

notes.front: Why does ΔG < 0 mean spontaneous? What is ΔG tracking?
notes.back: \(-\Delta G/T = \Delta S_{total}\) at constant T and P: ΔS of the system plus ΔS of surroundings (\(-\Delta H/T\)). ΔG < 0 means total entropy rises.
notes.extra: Pitfall: spontaneous says nothing about speed.

notes.front: Diamond → graphite and gasoline + O₂ → CO₂ are both spontaneous. Why do they not happen?
notes.back: ΔG < 0 only says the reaction is downhill. A high activation barrier makes the rate negligible at room temperature.
notes.analogy: A boulder on a ledge: it wants to fall, but a lip holds it until someone pushes.

notes.front: What is the difference between ΔG and ΔG°?
notes.back: ΔG° is for standard-state conditions (all activities 1). ΔG applies to actual conditions: \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q\). ΔG decides direction.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a positive ΔG° can still proceed if Q is small enough.

notes.front: \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\). At 25 °C, each factor of 10 in K corresponds to ΔG° of about {{c1::5.7 kJ/mol}}.
notes.text: \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\). At 25 °C, each factor of 10 in K corresponds to ΔG° of about {{c1::5.7 kJ/mol}}.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: ΔG° ≈ −30 kJ/mol gives K ≈ 10⁵ (essentially complete).

notes.front: How do you use Q compared with K?
notes.back: Q < K: the reaction proceeds forward. Q > K: it proceeds in reverse. Q = K: equilibrium. K only changes with temperature.
notes.analogy: A thermostat: Q is the room temperature, K is the setpoint.
notes.extra: Note: K says where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached.

notes.front: Why is the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, exothermic) run at ~450 °C, which seems to hurt yield?
notes.back: Low T favours NH₃ but is too slow even with an iron catalyst. High pressure (150–300 atm) and removing NH₃ by condensing recover the yield.
notes.analogy: A speed-versus-quality tradeoff: you accept lower per-pass yield to hit throughput.
notes.extra: Why pressure helps: 4 mol gas becomes 2.

notes.front: Why is carbon monoxide poisoning treated with pure oxygen?
notes.back: CO binds haemoglobin ~200× more tightly than O₂. Hb·CO + O₂ ⇌ Hb·O₂ + CO; flooding with O₂ shifts it back so CO is displaced.
notes.extra: Why it kills: bound CO also stops remaining haem from releasing O₂ properly.

notes.front: Why does a catalyst speed a reaction but not shift its equilibrium?
notes.back: It lowers the barrier equally for the forward and reverse reactions and leaves reactant and product energies alone, so K is unchanged.
notes.analogy: A second tunnel through the mountain: traffic flows faster both ways but the destination elevations are the same.

notes.front: What does the van 't Hoff equation predict about K when you heat a reaction?
notes.back: \(\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right)\). Endothermic: K rises. Exothermic: K falls.
notes.extra: Use: plot ln K vs 1/T; slope = −ΔH°/R.

notes.front: How does adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis drive biosynthesis whose ΔG is positive?
notes.back: The reactions are coupled through a shared intermediate (e.g. a phosphorylated substrate). ΔG° of hydrolysis ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol outweighs the +ve step so the total is negative.
notes.analogy: Crediting a spending account from a savings account so the purchase clears.
notes.extra: Note: in cells ΔG is ~−50 kJ/mol since ATP/adenosine diphosphate (ADP) is kept far from equilibrium.

notes.front: How does an Ellingham diagram show that carbon can smelt iron?
notes.back: It plots ΔG° of oxide formation vs T. The 2C + O₂ → 2CO line slopes down (gas created, ΔS > 0), crossing the Fe oxide lines at high T, so C wins above roughly 700 °C.
notes.extra: In practice: a blast furnace; the 'better' reductant is the lower line.

notes.front: What is the difference between kinetic and thermodynamic control?
notes.back: Kinetic: the product that forms fastest (lowest barrier) dominates, at low T, short time. Thermodynamic: reversibility lets the most stable product dominate at high T, long time.
notes.analogy: A quick win that ships first versus a better design that wins only if you can afford to iterate and rework.
notes.extra: Example: HBr + 1,3-butadiene: 1,2-adduct at −80 °C (kinetic), 1,4-adduct at 40 °C (thermodynamic).

notes.front: Why is true K defined with activities rather than concentrations?
notes.back: Real ions interact: \(a = \gamma c/c^\circ\). K from activities is dimensionless and constant; concentration ratios drift with ionic strength.
notes.extra: In practice: pH electrodes respond to H⁺ activity, and Debye–Hückel estimates γ.

notes.text: Three acid definitions: {{c1::Arrhenius}} (releases H⁺ in water), {{c2::Brønsted–Lowry}} (proton donor), {{c3::Lewis}} (electron-pair acceptor).
notes.extra: Use: Arrhenius for bench water chemistry; Brønsted for any proton transfer (even in ammonia or ethanol); Lewis for BF₃, AlCl₃ and metal ions binding ligands, where no proton moves.

notes.front: Why is pH a log scale, and what does one pH unit mean?
notes.back: \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]\). One unit is a 10× change in H⁺ concentration; pH 3 is 100× more acidic than pH 5.
notes.analogy: Like decibels or the Richter scale: it compresses a range spanning 14 orders of magnitude into numbers you can say aloud.
notes.extra: Pitfall: pH 6 to pH 5 is not 'a bit more acidic', it is ten times the H⁺.

notes.text: pH anchors: blood ≈ {{c1::7.4}}; stomach acid ≈ {{c2::1.5–3.5}}; vinegar ≈ {{c3::2.5}}; pure water at 25 °C = {{c4::7}}; household bleach ≈ {{c5::12.5}}.
notes.extra: Why it matters: blood is held within ~7.35–7.45; a drift of 0.3 units either way is life-threatening.

notes.front: Strong vs concentrated acid: what is the difference?
notes.back: Strength is how completely each molecule ionises (Ka). Concentration is how much acid per litre. They are independent.
notes.analogy: Strength is how willing each employee is to quit; concentration is how many employees there are.
notes.extra: Examples: 0.001 M HCl is strong but dilute; 17 M glacial acetic acid is weak but concentrated, and still burns skin.

notes.front: Why is HCl strong but acetic acid weak?
notes.back: HCl ionises essentially fully: Cl⁻ is a very poor base and won't take the proton back. Acetate is a decent base, so acetic acid sits mostly un-ionised (~1% in 0.1 M).
notes.extra: Rule: a strong acid has a negligible conjugate base; a weak acid has a conjugate base that really competes for H⁺. Conjugate pair = acid/base differing by one H⁺.

notes.front: What does pKa tell you about which way a proton goes?
notes.back: \(\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log K_a\). A proton moves from the lower-pKa acid to the conjugate base of the higher-pKa acid; the lower the pKa, the more it donates.
notes.analogy: Proton 'prices': the acid with the lower pKa sells its proton cheaply to whoever bids higher.
notes.extra: Example: acetic acid (4.76) protonates ammonia (NH₄⁺ pKa 9.25) almost completely: ΔpKa ≈ 4.5 means ~10⁴-fold lopsided.

notes.front: What is an amphoteric substance? Give two everyday examples.
notes.back: One that can act as acid or base depending on the partner. Water (H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂O ⇌ OH⁻) and aluminium hydroxide (dissolves in both acid and base).
notes.extra: Also: HCO₃⁻ and amino acids. This is why aluminium foil is attacked by both lye and strong acid.

notes.front: Why do the successive pKa values of a polyprotic acid (e.g. H₃PO₄: 2.2, 7.2, 12.4) climb?
notes.back: Pulling a proton off an already negative ion is harder (electrostatic attraction), so each step is a much weaker acid.
notes.analogy: Each step is harder than the last, like pulling a magnet off a stack where the remaining pile is charged opposite to the proton.
notes.extra: In practice: cola's phosphoric acid is mainly the first step; phosphate buffers at pH 7.2 work around the second.

notes.front: Why do baking soda + vinegar fizz, and how is that the same as an antacid?
notes.back: Bicarbonate takes a proton: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂↑. An antacid (CaCO₃, NaHCO₃, Mg(OH)₂) is a weak base neutralising stomach HCl.
notes.extra: Gas: the fizz is CO₂ escaping because carbonic acid is unstable. Burping after bicarbonate is the same bubbles.

notes.front: What makes acid rain acid, given that clean rain already has pH ~5.6?
notes.back: Clean rain is mildly acidic from dissolved CO₂ (carbonic acid). SO₂ and NOₓ from burning fuel oxidise to H₂SO₄ and HNO₃, dropping pH below 5.6.
notes.extra: Damage: marble and limestone (CaCO₃) dissolve; power stations scrub SO₂ with limestone, producing gypsum.

notes.front: Why must bleach and ammonia never be mixed?
notes.back: Hypochlorite oxidises ammonia to chloramines (NH₂Cl, NHCl₂, NCl₃), toxic gases that damage lungs. Bleach plus acid releases chlorine gas, equally bad.
notes.extra: Pitfall: 'extra strength' cleaning by combining products is how most accidents happen; ventilation does not make it safe.

notes.front: What is a buffer, and what does the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation say?
notes.back: A weak acid plus its conjugate base resists pH change. \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\).
notes.analogy: A shock absorber with two reservoirs: HA soaks up added base, A⁻ soaks up added acid.
notes.extra: Best range: pH = pKa ± 1, where both forms are present. At pH = pKa they are 1:1 and capacity is highest.

notes.front: How does the bicarbonate buffer hold blood at 7.4, and why does hyperventilating shift it?
notes.back: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; with [HCO₃⁻]:[CO₂] ≈ 20:1, pH = 6.1 + log 20 ≈ 7.4. Lungs set CO₂, so breathing sets pH.
notes.analogy: Lungs are the pH knob: exhale CO₂ and the acid side drains away.
notes.extra: In practice: hyperventilating blows off CO₂, raising pH (tingling, dizziness); breathing into a bag restores CO₂.

notes.front: In a titration, why use phenolphthalein for acetic acid + NaOH, and how do equivalence point and endpoint differ?
notes.back: Equivalence is where moles of base equal moles of acid (pH ~8.7 here); endpoint is where the indicator changes (phenolphthalein turns pink at pH 8.2–10), chosen to bracket it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: for a strong acid + strong base equivalence is pH 7, so many indicators work; for a weak acid + strong base the jump sits above 7, so methyl orange (3.1–4.4) would fail.

notes.front: What is an oxidation state, and what does it tell you about a reaction?
notes.back: A bookkeeping charge assigning shared electrons to the more electronegative atom. Redox = any reaction where oxidation states change; oxidation loses electrons, reduction gains (OIL RIG).
notes.analogy: Ledger entries, not real money: the numbers track where electrons are credited, even in covalent molecules.
notes.extra: Example: C in CH₄ is −4, in CO₂ +4. Burning methane moves 8 electrons per carbon.

notes.front: Galvanic vs electrolytic cell: what is the key difference?
notes.back: Galvanic: spontaneous reaction produces electrical energy (battery), cathode positive. Electrolytic: external power drives a non-spontaneous reaction (plating, charging), cathode negative.
notes.extra: Constant in both: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Only the sign flips; a rechargeable battery is galvanic discharging, electrolytic charging.

notes.front: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, which way do electrons flow, and what does the salt bridge do?
notes.back: Electrons flow through the wire from Zn (anode, oxidised) to Cu (cathode, reduced). The salt bridge's ions migrate to balance charge, closing the circuit.
notes.analogy: Wire is the express lane for electrons; the salt bridge is the return road for ions. Block either and the cell stops.
notes.extra: Half-reactions: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Cell potential E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

notes.front: What does the Nernst equation add to a standard potential, and where does a pH meter use it?
notes.back: \(E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q\): potential shifts with concentrations. At 25 °C a glass electrode gives ~59 mV per pH unit.
notes.extra: Link: \(\Delta G = -nFE\). F ≈ 96,485 C/mol. Glucose strips measure current via an enzyme, not a Nernst potential, but ion-selective electrodes do.

notes.front: Why do batteries sag in the cold, when the Nernst voltage barely changes?
notes.back: It's kinetics, not thermodynamics: ion transport and electrode reactions slow (Arrhenius), the electrolyte thickens, internal resistance rises, so the voltage under load drops.
notes.analogy: The fuel tank holds as much as before, but the fuel line is frozen.
notes.extra: Example: lead–acid cold-cranking amps fall sharply near −20 °C; keep phone and EV batteries warm.

notes.front: Why does galvanising (zinc coating) protect steel even when scratched?
notes.back: Zinc is more easily oxidised than iron (E° −0.76 V vs −0.44 V), so it acts as a sacrificial anode: zinc corrodes, iron stays as the cathode.
notes.extra: Contrast: tin-plated cans protect only while intact; tin is less reactive than iron, so a scratch makes the iron the anode and speeds rusting.

notes.front: Why is rust an electrochemical cell, and why does salt speed it up?
notes.back: A wet iron surface has anodic spots (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) and cathodic spots (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). Water plus dissolved ions completes the circuit; salt makes the water a better conductor.
notes.extra: Product: Fe(OH)₂ is oxidised to hydrated Fe₂O₃, flaky and porous, so it doesn't protect the metal beneath.

notes.front: Why don't aluminium and stainless steel rust like iron, even though they're reactive?
notes.back: Passivation: a thin, tight, self-healing oxide film (Al₂O₃; Cr₂O₃-rich on steel with ≥10.5% Cr) blocks further attack. Rust is porous and flakes off.
notes.analogy: A coat of paint that re-applies itself whenever scratched in air.
notes.extra: Breaks down: chloride (salt water, bleach) punctures the film, causing pitting in stainless steel and aluminium alike.

notes.front: How do chlor-alkali and aluminium smelting use electrolysis, and why not simply electrolyse aqueous Al³⁺?
notes.back: Brine gives Cl₂, H₂ and NaOH. Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite at ~960 °C because in water H₂ forms before Al metal would.
notes.extra: Cost: aluminium needs ~13–15 kWh per kg, so smelters sit beside cheap power; recycling uses ~5% of that energy. A fuel cell is this process run in reverse.

notes.front: How does a lithium-ion cell store charge, and why do they fail when over-discharged or abused?
notes.back: Li⁺ ions shuttle between graphite (anode, intercalated as LiC₆) and a metal-oxide cathode; the crystals stay intact, so no deposition. Over-discharge or overcharge damages electrodes and can trigger thermal runaway.
notes.analogy: A rocking-chair: ions are guests moving between two hotels, not consumed.
notes.extra: Fire: the flammable organic electrolyte plus oxygen released from a hot cathode; lithium plating shorts the cell.

notes.front: What is overpotential, and why does chlor-alkali make Cl₂ rather than O₂ at the anode?
notes.back: Overpotential η is the extra voltage beyond E° needed to drive a reaction at useful rate (kinetic barrier at the electrode). O₂ evolution has a large η, so Cl₂ wins despite its higher E°.
notes.extra: Tafel: \(\eta = a + b\log j\). Water splits at 1.23 V in theory, ~1.5–2 V in practice.

notes.front: What does a Pourbaix diagram show, and what can't it tell you?
notes.back: Potential versus pH maps of which species of an element is thermodynamically stable (immunity, corrosion, passivation). It says nothing about speed.
notes.extra: Example: iron in high-pH concrete sits in the passive region; carbonation drops the pH and the rebar rusts.

notes.front: Thermodynamics vs kinetics: what does each tell you about a reaction?
notes.back: Thermodynamics (ΔG) says whether a reaction can go and how far; kinetics says how fast. A favourable reaction can be effectively frozen.
notes.analogy: Gravity says the ball should roll downhill; kinetics asks whether there's a hump in the way.
notes.extra: Example: diamond → graphite is favourable, but the barrier is enormous, so diamonds last forever at room temperature.

notes.front: What is a rate law, and why can't you read it off the balanced equation?
notes.back: An experimentally determined equation, \(\text{rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n\), where orders m and n come from the mechanism, not the stoichiometry.
notes.extra: Example: NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ at low T has rate = k[NO₂]², with no CO term.

notes.front: Why is alcohol metabolism zero order, and what does that mean for the rate of clearing?
notes.back: At typical doses liver alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated, so it works at its maximum: a constant amount is removed per hour, independent of concentration.
notes.analogy: A single checkout lane with a long queue: it clears customers at a fixed pace however many are waiting.
notes.extra: In practice: roughly one drink per hour; coffee or a shower doesn't speed it up.

notes.front: What does first-order kinetics look like for drugs and radioactive decay?
notes.back: The rate is proportional to the amount present, giving exponential decay: a fixed fraction goes per unit time, so half-life \(t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k\) is constant.
notes.extra: Example: caffeine's half-life is ~5 h: after 10 h a quarter remains. After about 5 half-lives, ~3% is left.

notes.text: Half-life by order: for a {{c1::first}}-order reaction it is constant; for {{c2::zero}} order it {{c3::shortens}} as the reactant is used up; for {{c4::second}} order it {{c5::lengthens}}.
notes.extra: Why: a second-order reaction slows as the reactant thins (fewer collisions); zero order runs at a fixed rate until the supply ends.

notes.front: What does the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\) say?
notes.back: The rate constant grows exponentially with temperature, because the fraction of molecules above the activation energy rises. Plot ln k vs 1/T: slope −Eₐ/R.
notes.analogy: Raising T doesn't make everyone faster, it makes the rare molecules clearing the barrier far more numerous.
notes.extra: Terms: A is the attempt frequency (collisions with proper orientation).

notes.front: Where does the rule of thumb '10 °C doubles the rate' come from, and where does it fail?
notes.back: For Eₐ ≈ 50 kJ/mol near room temperature, k rises ~1.9× per 10 °C. Higher Eₐ gives bigger factors, lower gives less.
notes.extra: In practice: a 4 °C fridge slows spoilage ~3-fold vs 20 °C; cold also slows rusting; fever speeds enzymes. Not valid when an enzyme denatures.

notes.front: What is activation energy, and what is the transition state?
notes.back: Eₐ is the energy barrier between reactants and products. The transition state is the highest-energy arrangement along the path, caught momentarily.
notes.analogy: The pass over a mountain: how steep the climb is matters, not how deep the valley beyond.
notes.extra: Lifetime: about one bond vibration, ~10⁻¹³ s. It can't be bottled.

notes.front: According to collision theory, what must happen for a collision to react, and why does surface area matter?
notes.back: Molecules must collide with at least Eₐ and the right orientation. Finer powder exposes more surface, so more collisions per second.
notes.extra: In practice: flour and sugar dust explode as clouds but a sugar cube only chars; powdered sugar dissolves faster than a lump.

notes.front: What is a reaction mechanism, and how do elementary steps relate to rate laws?
notes.back: A mechanism is the sequence of elementary steps. For an elementary step only, the rate law follows its molecularity (unimolecular, bimolecular).
notes.extra: Test: a proposed mechanism must sum to the overall equation and predict the observed rate law.

notes.front: What is the rate-determining step, and how does it shape the rate law?
notes.back: The slowest step is the bottleneck. The overall rate follows the species up to and including it; later steps don't appear.
notes.analogy: The narrowest pipe in a pipeline, or the slowest stage in a CI build: the whole throughput is set by it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: 'slowest' means highest effective barrier, which need not be the single highest peak.

notes.front: Intermediate vs transition state: how do they differ?
notes.back: An intermediate is a real species in an energy valley with a finite lifetime (sometimes isolable). A transition state is a peak, the saddle point, with no lifetime.
notes.extra: Test: intermediates appear as dips on a profile, TS as maxima. Two-step reactions have one intermediate and two transition states.

notes.front: What is the steady-state approximation?
notes.back: A reactive intermediate is consumed as fast as made, so its concentration stays tiny and \(d[I]/dt \approx 0\); use this to derive the rate law.
notes.analogy: A queue whose arrivals match departures: the line stays short and constant.
notes.extra: Used in: enzyme kinetics (Briggs–Haldane) and radical chains.

notes.front: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction without being used up?
notes.back: It offers an alternative pathway with a lower activation barrier, binding reactants and then releasing products, so it is regenerated and a little goes a long way.
notes.analogy: A tunnel through the mountain: the start and end altitudes are the same, the climb is gone.
notes.extra: Why: if it shifted equilibrium it would give free work.

notes.front: Homogeneous vs heterogeneous catalysis: what is the difference, and why does a catalytic converter use the latter?
notes.back: Homogeneous: catalyst in the same phase as reactants. Heterogeneous: different phase, usually a solid surface. Converters coat Pt/Pd/Rh on a ceramic honeycomb for gas contact.
notes.extra: Job: turns CO, NOₓ and unburnt hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂ and H₂O. Heterogeneous catalysts are easy to separate; leaded fuel poisons them.

notes.text: Industrial catalysts: Haber ammonia uses {{c1::iron}}; car converters use {{c2::platinum, palladium and rhodium}}; low-pressure polyethylene uses {{c3::Ziegler–Natta (TiCl₄ + aluminium alkyl)}}.
notes.extra: Haber: splitting N≡N on the iron surface is the slow step. Ziegler–Natta: controls chain stereochemistry (isotactic polypropylene).

notes.front: What do Km and Vmax mean in \(v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m+[S])\)?
notes.back: Vmax is the top speed when all enzyme is saturated with substrate. Km is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax; low Km means tight binding.
notes.analogy: Toll booths: once every booth is busy, more cars don't raise throughput. Km is the traffic at which half of them are in use.
notes.extra: Zero order: at [S] ≫ Km, which explains alcohol metabolism; first order at [S] ≪ Km.

notes.front: Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition: how do they change Km and Vmax?
notes.back: Competitive: inhibitor fights for the active site, Km rises, Vmax unchanged (more substrate overcomes it). Non-competitive: binds elsewhere, Vmax falls, Km unchanged.
notes.extra: Memory: competitive can be outcompeted; non-competitive effectively removes enzyme molecules.

notes.front: Why is ethanol given to treat methanol poisoning?
notes.back: Alcohol dehydrogenase binds ethanol more strongly than methanol (competitive inhibition), so methanol isn't turned into toxic formaldehyde and formic acid but excreted.
notes.extra: Modern option: fomepizole blocks the enzyme directly. Methanol damage causes blindness and acidosis.

notes.front: What is autocatalysis, and how can it produce oscillating reactions?
notes.back: A product catalyses its own formation: slow start, then a sudden burst (S-shaped curve). With delayed negative feedback this can cycle, as in the Belousov–Zhabotinsky colour oscillation.
notes.analogy: A viral post: slow at first, then every reader makes more readers.
notes.extra: Example: Mn²⁺ catalyses KMnO₄ + oxalate, so the purple fades abruptly after a lag.

notes.front: What are the stages of a chain reaction, and how do chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) destroy ozone?
notes.back: Initiation makes radicals, propagation regenerates them, termination removes them. UV frees Cl• from CFCs; Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂.
notes.analogy: A chain letter: each recipient forwards to another, until the letters meet and cancel.
notes.extra: Scale: one Cl• destroys ~10⁵ ozone molecules. Same pattern drives radical polymerisation and methane chlorination.

notes.front: Why do antioxidants (such as butylated hydroxytoluene, BHT, and vitamin E) stop fats going rancid?
notes.back: Rancidity is a radical chain. Antioxidants donate an H atom to chain-carrying peroxyl radicals, producing an unreactive radical that cannot propagate: a chain terminator.
notes.extra: In practice: BHT in cereal and oils. They are consumed in the process, so protection is finite.

notes.front: What does the Hammond postulate say, and how does it explain why bromination is more selective than chlorination?
notes.back: A transition state resembles its closer-energy neighbour. Exothermic steps have early, reactant-like TS; endothermic steps have late, product-like TS.
notes.extra: Example: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its late TS feels the stability of the radical being formed and strongly prefers tertiary C–H.

notes.front: What is the kinetic isotope effect, and what does a large kH/kD tell you?
notes.back: C–D bonds react slower than C–H because deuterium's lower zero-point energy raises the effective barrier. kH/kD of ~2–7 means C–H breaks in the rate-determining step.
notes.extra: Use: a mechanism probe; also deuterated drugs resist metabolism and last longer.

notes.front: What does Marcus theory predict about electron transfer, including the inverted region?
notes.back: \(\Delta G^\ddagger = (\lambda+\Delta G^\circ)^2/4\lambda\), where λ is reorganisation energy. Rate rises with driving force until −ΔG° > λ, then falls.
notes.analogy: A throw that's too forceful overshoots the target.
notes.extra: Why it matters: photosynthesis exploits it to slow back-transfer and keep charge separated.

notes.front: How does the Eyring equation improve on Arrhenius?
notes.back: \(k = \frac{k_BT}{h}e^{-\Delta G^\ddagger/RT}\) from transition-state theory, splitting the barrier into ΔH‡ and ΔS‡. Arrhenius's A and Eₐ are empirical; here Eₐ ≈ ΔH‡ + RT.
notes.extra: Insight: a negative ΔS‡ (two molecules joining into a tight TS) shows up as a low pre-exponential factor. k_BT/h ≈ 6×10¹² s⁻¹ at 300 K.

notes.front: Why is carbon the element of life and not, say, silicon?
notes.back: Carbon makes four strong bonds and, uniquely, strong C–C bonds that chain and ring; it also bonds firmly to H, O, N. Si–Si and Si–O chains are weaker or too inert/too stable.
notes.analogy: Carbon is the Lego brick with four studs that clicks hard to itself and to everything else; silicon's bricks either don't hold or fuse into a solid block (sand).
notes.extra: Numbers: C–C ≈ 350 kJ/mol, Si–Si ≈ 220 kJ/mol; Si–O ≈ 450 so silicon prefers rock (SiO₂) to chains.

notes.front: Why are alkanes so unreactive (the 'paraffins', from 'little affinity')?
notes.back: Only strong, nonpolar C–C and C–H σ bonds: no lone pairs, no π bond, no partial charges for a reagent to attack. They react only with O₂ (burning) and radicals.
notes.extra: In practice: that inertness is why wax, mineral oil and petrol keep for years, and why they are good solvents for other nonpolar things.

notes.front: Petrol, diesel, candle wax: how do they differ chemically, and why does it change their behaviour?
notes.back: Chain length. Petrol ≈ C₅–C₁₀ (volatile), diesel ≈ C₁₀–C₁₆ (oily), wax ≈ C₂₀+ (solid). Longer chains = more London dispersion = higher boiling/melting point.
notes.analogy: Velcro strips: the longer the strip, the more it clings to its neighbours.
notes.extra: In practice: refineries separate them by boiling point in a fractionating column, then crack long chains into short ones.

notes.text: Group → everyday example: alcohol {{c1::ethanol (drinks, hand gel)}}; ketone {{c2::acetone (nail polish remover)}}; aldehyde {{c3::formaldehyde (preservative)}}; carboxylic acid {{c4::acetic acid (vinegar)}}.
notes.extra: Esters (RCOOR′) are the fruit smells: isoamyl acetate = banana. Aldehyde = C=O at chain end; ketone = in the middle.

notes.front: Amine vs amide: both contain N, so why is an amine basic but an amide not?
notes.back: An amine's N lone pair is free to grab H⁺. In an amide it is delocalised into the neighbouring C=O, so it is unavailable.
notes.analogy: A tap that is open (amine) versus a tap whose water is already diverted into another pipe (amide).
notes.extra: Consequence: the peptide bond is an amide: planar, stable, not basic. Caffeine and aspirin also mix groups (aspirin: ester + acid).

notes.front: How do you read a label name like 'ethanol', 'propanone', 'butanoic acid'?
notes.back: Stem = carbon count (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-), ending = group: -ol alcohol, -al aldehyde, -one ketone, -oic acid, -oate ester, -amine amine.
notes.extra: Use: 'sodium benzoate' on a food label is the salt of benzoic acid; '-ene' means a C=C, '-yne' a C≡C.

notes.front: What are cis/trans (geometric) isomers, and what do trans fats have to do with them?
notes.back: A C=C cannot rotate, so groups stay on the same (cis) or opposite (trans) side. Natural unsaturated fats are cis (kinked); partial hydrogenation makes straight trans fats that pack like saturated fat.
notes.extra: Why it matters: trans fats raise low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and are solid-ish at room temperature, which is why industry wanted them.

notes.front: Why did thalidomide teach drug makers about enantiomers?
notes.back: Its two mirror-image forms act differently in the body: one sedates, the other is teratogenic. Because it racemises in the body, giving only the 'safe' one would not have helped.
notes.extra: Lesson: a chiral drug must be tested enantiomer by enantiomer; today many are sold as single enantiomers.

notes.front: Why can your nose tell (R)- from (S)-carvone (spearmint vs caraway), and why are protein amino acids all L?
notes.back: Enantiomers have identical physical properties but interact differently with other chiral things. Smell receptors and enzymes are made of L-amino acids, so they are chiral 'locks'.
notes.analogy: A right-handed screw fits a right-handed thread only.
notes.extra: Chiral: a carbon with four different groups is a stereocentre. Enantiomers differ only in a chiral environment (polarised light, receptors).

notes.front: Why does cyclohexane adopt a chair, and what are axial and equatorial positions?
notes.back: The chair keeps all C–C–C angles ≈ 109.5° and all H staggered. Axial bonds run parallel to the ring axis; equatorial point outward. Bulky groups prefer equatorial (avoid 1,3-diaxial clashes).
notes.extra: Number: methyl equatorial is favoured by ~7 kJ/mol; the ring flips at room temperature in microseconds.

notes.front: Why is cyclopropane strained and reactive?
notes.back: Its C–C–C angle is 60° versus the ideal 109.5°, so bonds are bent ('banana' bonds) and eclipsed. About 115 kJ/mol of strain is released on ring opening.
notes.extra: Contrast: cyclohexane in a chair is essentially strain-free.

notes.front: What does a curly arrow show in a mechanism?
notes.back: The movement of an electron pair (full head) or single electron (fishhook), from a source (lone pair or bond) to a sink (an atom that can accept it). Never the movement of atoms.
notes.extra: Rule: arrows start at electrons and end where they will sit; charge and octets must balance.

notes.front: Nucleophile vs electrophile: what is the difference?
notes.back: Nucleophile: electron-rich, donates a pair (HO⁻, NH₃, CN⁻). Electrophile: electron-poor, accepts a pair (carbonyl C, H⁺, alkyl halide C). Nearly every polar reaction is one meeting the other.
notes.analogy: Producer and consumer: one has electrons to give, the other has an open slot.
notes.extra: Pitfall: basicity is thermodynamic (binds H⁺); nucleophilicity is kinetic (attacks C). Related but not the same.

notes.front: Inductive vs resonance effect: how do they differ?
notes.back: Inductive: polarisation through σ bonds by electronegativity, fading fast with distance. Resonance: delocalisation of π/lone-pair electrons across conjugation, working at long range.
notes.analogy: Inductive is a smell drifting through the air and thinning out; resonance is a pipe carrying the flow far.
notes.extra: Example: Cl–CH₂–COOH (pKa 2.9) is more acidic than acetic acid (4.8) by induction; the NO₂ in nitrophenol acts by resonance.

notes.front: Why are tertiary carbocations more stable than primary ones?
notes.back: Alkyl groups donate electrons by induction and by hyperconjugation (σ C–H electrons overlap the empty p orbital), spreading the charge. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
notes.extra: Hyperconjugation: more adjacent C–H bonds, more donation; the same effect makes more-substituted alkenes more stable (Zaitsev).

notes.front: Why does benzene not add Br₂ like an alkene does, and what is Hückel's rule?
notes.back: Addition would destroy the delocalised π sextet (~150 kJ/mol stabilisation), so it substitutes (keeps the ring). Hückel: a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with 4n+2 π electrons is aromatic.
notes.extra: Contrast: cyclobutadiene (4 π e⁻) is antiaromatic and unstable; benzene needs a Lewis acid to react.

notes.text: Approx. pKa ladder: alkane {{c1::~50}}; alcohol/water {{c2::~16}}; phenol {{c3::~10}}; carboxylic acid {{c4::~5}}.
notes.extra: Read it as: a lower pKa is a stronger acid; each unit is a factor of 10 in Ka.

notes.front: Why are phenol and carboxylic acids acidic but ethanol barely?
notes.back: Acidity is set by the stability of the conjugate base. Phenoxide delocalises charge into the ring; carboxylate shares it equally over two O. Ethoxide keeps charge on one O.
notes.extra: Scale: carboxylic acid vs alcohol is ~10¹¹ in Ka, and that gap is delocalisation.

notes.front: SN1 vs SN2: how do you tell which operates?
notes.back: SN2 (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution): one step, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion, favoured by methyl/1° substrates, strong Nu, polar aprotic solvent. SN1 (unimolecular nucleophilic substitution): carbocation first, rate = k[RX], racemisation, 3° substrates, weak Nu, polar protic solvent.
notes.analogy: SN2 is a handover in a single step; SN1 is two stages with a temporary hold.
notes.extra: Why solvent matters: protic solvents H-bond to and 'cage' Nu⁻ (slowing SN2) and stabilise the carbocation (speeding SN1).

notes.front: E2 vs E1: how do they differ, and why does heat favour elimination over substitution?
notes.back: E2 (bimolecular elimination): one step, needs strong base, H and leaving group anti-periplanar. E1 (unimolecular elimination): carbocation first, then loss of H⁺ (competes with SN1, unimolecular nucleophilic substitution). Heat favours elimination because it makes more molecules (ΔS > 0).
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: strong, hindered base + heat → E2; weak base, ionising solvent → SN1/E1.

notes.front: Zaitsev vs Hofmann elimination: which alkene forms and when?
notes.back: Zaitsev: the more substituted (more stable) alkene, with small bases like ethoxide. Hofmann: the less substituted alkene, with a bulky base (t-BuOK) that reaches only the accessible H.

notes.front: What is Markovnikov's rule for HBr adding to an alkene, and why?
notes.back: H adds to the carbon with more H's, Br to the more substituted carbon. Reason: the protonation gives the more stable (more substituted) carbocation, so that pathway is faster.
notes.extra: Exception: with peroxides HBr adds by a radical chain and reverses (anti-Markovnikov).

notes.front: How does a radical chain reaction work (e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ under light), and why is Br• more selective than Cl•?
notes.back: Initiation (light splits Cl₂), propagation (Cl• takes H, R• takes Cl, regenerating Cl•), termination (two radicals combine). Br• abstraction is endothermic with a late transition state, so it prefers the weakest C–H (Hammond).
notes.analogy: A chain letter: each recipient sends it on until the copies run out.
notes.extra: In practice: antioxidants (such as butylated hydroxytoluene, BHT, and vitamin E) stop food and plastics going rancid by breaking these chains.

notes.front: What does the Hammett equation \(\log(K/K_0)=\sigma\rho\) tell you?
notes.back: σ measures a substituent's electron donor/acceptor power (p-NO₂ = +0.78, p-OMe = −0.27); ρ measures how sensitive a reaction is to it. The sign of ρ shows whether charge builds (+) or is lost (−) in the transition state.
notes.analogy: A linear regression of rate against substituent strength: slope ρ = how much the reaction cares.

notes.front: What is the Curtin–Hammett principle?
notes.back: If conformers interconvert faster than they react, the product ratio is set by the difference in transition-state energies, not by the populations of the conformers.
notes.analogy: Many queues feeding one checkout: the outcome depends on the slowest gate to pass, not on how many wait at each.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the less abundant conformer can give the major product.

notes.front: In frontier molecular orbital (FMO) theory, which orbitals decide a reaction?
notes.back: The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of the nucleophile (electron donor) interacts with the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of the electrophile (acceptor). Reactivity depends on their overlap and a small energy gap.
notes.analogy: Source and target: a sender only matters where the receiver has an open port.
notes.extra: Success: explains why Nu attacks the C of C=O (large LUMO coefficient) and underpins Diels–Alder selectivity.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why is the carbon of a carbonyl (C=O) electrophilic, and what happens when a nucleophile meets it?
notes.back: Oxygen pulls the π electrons, so C is δ+. Nu attacks it (at ~107° to the plane, the Bürgi–Dunitz angle), pushing the π pair onto O to give a tetrahedral alkoxide.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones?
notes.back: Sterics: one H instead of a second bulky R makes attack easier. Electronics: a ketone's two alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilise the C=O, making it less electrophilic.
notes.extra: In practice: aldehydes oxidise easily to acids (they smell and tarnish), ketones like acetone are tough.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How do hemiacetals and acetals link to sugars?
notes.back: Aldehyde + alcohol gives a hemiacetal; acid and a second alcohol gives an acetal. Glucose's own OH closes onto its CHO to form a ring, and sugars join through acetal (glycosidic) links into starch and cellulose.
notes.extra: Chemist's trick: acetals survive base and Grignards, so they protect carbonyls.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why must a Grignard reagent (RMgBr) be made and used in dry ether?
notes.back: R–Mg is essentially R⁻, a very strong base (pKa of R–H ≈ 50). Water or alcohol instantly protonates it to the alkane, destroying the reagent; ether solvates the Mg.
notes.extra: Use: RMgBr + carbonyl forms a new C–C bond, the classic route to alcohols.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.text: Acyl reactivity ladder: {{c1::acyl chloride}} > {{c2::anhydride}} > {{c3::ester}} > {{c4::amide}}.
notes.extra: Why: a better leaving group (Cl⁻) and weaker resonance donation from the substituent mean higher reactivity.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why are amides so stable, and why does that matter for life?
notes.back: The N lone pair delocalises into C=O (partial double bond, planar, poor leaving group). Peptide bonds therefore last for years in water, but enzymes (proteases) cut them quickly.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How does saponification make soap, and why is it irreversible?
notes.back: Fat (a triglyceride) + NaOH hydrolyses to glycerol and fatty-acid carboxylate salts (soap). The carboxylate is a poor electrophile, so the reverse can't occur.
notes.extra: Related: biodiesel is transesterification (oil + methanol, NaOH gives methyl esters + glycerol). Soap works by micelles: tail in grease, head in water.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What is an aldol reaction, and why does nature depend on this type of chemistry?
notes.back: An enolate (made from a carbonyl's acidic α-H) attacks another carbonyl, forming a C–C bond and a β-hydroxy carbonyl. Biology builds carbon skeletons this way; the Claisen version builds fatty acids two carbons at a time.
notes.analogy: Building a chain by snapping on identical two-carbon blocks.
notes.extra: Why even numbers: fatty acids are built from acetyl-CoA, so chains are even in length.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Maillard reaction vs caramelisation: what is the difference?
notes.back: Maillard: amino groups (proteins) + reducing sugars at ~140–165 °C produce brown pigments and flavour (steak, bread crust). Caramelisation: sugar alone is pyrolysed.
notes.extra: In practice: dry the surface of meat before searing; water keeps it near 100 °C and stops browning.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What is a Diels–Alder reaction, and what makes it special?
notes.back: A diene (4 π e⁻) plus a dienophile (2 π e⁻) forms a cyclohexene in one concerted step: two new C–C bonds, 100% atom economy, defined stereochemistry.
notes.extra: Fastest when: an electron-rich diene meets an electron-poor dienophile (the gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is small).

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What do the Woodward–Hoffmann rules say?
notes.back: A pericyclic reaction is thermally allowed when the number of electrons is 4n+2 (suprafacially), photochemically for 4n. Diels–Alder ([4+2], 6 e⁻) is thermal; [2+2] needs light.
notes.extra: Why: orbital symmetry must be conserved between highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO); forbidden reactions have a high barrier.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How do the oxidation levels of carbon progress, with an everyday example?
notes.back: Alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid → CO₂ (more bonds to O, fewer to H). Wine turns to vinegar when Acetobacter oxidises ethanol to acetic acid with air.
notes.extra: Breathalyser: orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ turns green Cr³⁺ as it oxidises ethanol (older devices; modern ones use fuel cells). Tertiary alcohols resist.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: NaBH₄ vs LiAlH₄: how do they differ?
notes.back: NaBH₄ is mild: reduces aldehydes and ketones, works in alcohol/water. LiAlH₄ is far stronger: also reduces esters, acids, amides, and reacts violently with water.
notes.extra: Why it matters: NaBH₄ reduces a ketone in a molecule while leaving an ester untouched (chemoselectivity).

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why does hydrogenation turn liquid oils into margarine?
notes.back: H₂ with a Ni catalyst saturates the C=C bonds. Kinks disappear, chains pack better and the melting point rises, so the oil becomes spreadable.
notes.extra: Pitfall: partial hydrogenation also isomerises some cis to trans, the origin of trans fats.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What is retrosynthesis and the logic of protecting groups?
notes.back: Work backwards from the target: disconnect a bond into simple, available pieces (Corey). A protecting group masks one reactive site (e.g. an acetal on a ketone) so a reagent attacks only the other.
notes.analogy: Planning a route from the destination backwards; protection is a temporary road closure.
notes.extra: Cost: each protect/deprotect step adds yield loss and waste, so good routes avoid them.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why did palladium cross-coupling (Suzuki, Heck) earn a Nobel Prize and underpin pharma?
notes.back: It joins two carbon fragments (e.g. aryl–aryl) under mild conditions with tolerance for other groups. Cycle: oxidative addition, transmetalation, reductive elimination.
notes.analogy: A universal connector that snaps two complex components together without disturbing the rest.
notes.extra: In practice: biaryl cores of many drugs are made by Suzuki coupling (ArB(OH)₂ + Ar′X, Pd, base).

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why do chemists need asymmetric catalysis (Noyori, Sharpless)?
notes.back: Because a drug's enantiomers can differ in effect. A small chiral catalyst makes mostly one enantiomer, so one catalyst molecule can steer millions of product molecules.
notes.extra: Examples: Noyori's chiral hydrogenation; Sharpless's epoxidation of allylic alcohols.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What is atom economy, and why does it matter for green chemistry?
notes.back: Atom economy = (molar mass of desired product) / (molar mass of all reactants) × 100. High values mean little waste (Diels–Alder: 100%), unlike routes that make stoichiometric by-products.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How are aspirin and paracetamol made, and why use acetic anhydride?
notes.back: Aspirin: salicylic acid + acetic anhydride (acetylates the phenol OH). Paracetamol: 4-aminophenol + acetic anhydride (acetylates N, which is more nucleophilic than O). The anhydride is far more reactive than acetic acid.
notes.extra: By-product: acetic acid, so you smell vinegar from old aspirin.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.text: Infrared (IR): a strong peak at {{c1::~1700 cm⁻¹}} means C=O; a broad band at {{c2::3200–3550 cm⁻¹}} means alcohol O–H; a very broad band {{c3::2500–3300 cm⁻¹}} means a carboxylic acid O–H.
notes.extra: Why broad: hydrogen bonding gives a range of O–H bond strengths, smearing the peak.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How do you read a ¹H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum for a structure?
notes.back: Shift tells the environment (deshielded H near O or C=O sit downfield), integration gives the H count, and splitting (n+1 rule) gives the neighbouring H count. Ethanol: CH₃ triplet, CH₂ quartet, O–H singlet, in a 3:2:1 ratio.
notes.analogy: Postcode, headcount and neighbours for each hydrogen.
notes.extra: Tetramethylsilane (TMS): 12 equivalent H, one sharp signal at 0, inert. CDCl₃: no ¹H to swamp the sample; its D gives the field lock (residual CHCl₃ at 7.26).

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
