notes.front: What does ¹³C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) tell you that ¹H NMR does not?
notes.back: The carbon skeleton: one signal per distinct carbon. Shifts: C=O ≈ 170–210, aromatic ≈ 110–160, alkyl ≈ 0–50 ppm. It is weak because only 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: In mass spectrometry, how do you recognise Cl or Br from the M and M+2 peaks?
notes.back: Cl gives M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1 (³⁵Cl:³⁷Cl); Br gives ≈ 1 : 1 (⁷⁹Br:⁸¹Br). The molecular ion gives the mass; fragments (loss of 15, 18, 29) show the pieces.
notes.extra: Nitrogen rule: an odd molecular mass implies an odd number of N atoms.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: Why are carrots orange, and how does conjugation relate to sunscreens?
notes.back: β-Carotene has 11 conjugated C=C. More conjugation shrinks the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO)–lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) gap, so absorption moves to visible blue light and carrots look orange. Sunscreen filters are conjugated molecules tuned to absorb UV.
notes.analogy: A longer string vibrates at lower pitch: more conjugation absorbs lower-energy light.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: How do you combine mass spectrometry (MS), infrared (IR) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) to identify an unknown?
notes.back: MS gives the formula/mass, IR the functional groups, ¹³C the carbon environments, ¹H the H count and connectivity. Use the degree of unsaturation to test the proposal, then check every peak.
notes.analogy: Detective work: each technique is a witness; the structure must satisfy all of them.
notes.extra: Degree of unsaturation: (2C+2+N−H−X)/2 counts rings plus π bonds.

notes.deck: Chemistry::08 Organic Synthesis, Spectroscopy & Natural Products
notes.front: What do correlation spectroscopy (COSY) and heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) add to a crowded nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum?
notes.back: COSY maps which H couple with which (neighbours, 2–3 bonds). HSQC links each H to the carbon it is directly bonded to. Together they trace a molecule's connectivity.
notes.analogy: A dependency graph: COSY draws the H–H edges, HSQC joins each H to its C.

notes.front: Why is atmospheric N₂ so unreactive, and why does fertiliser therefore need the Haber process?
notes.back: N≡N is a triple bond of ~945 kJ/mol, with no dipole and a huge highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO)–lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) gap. Plants cannot use N₂; Haber forces it to react with H₂ over iron.
notes.analogy: A treasure chest with an enormous lock: the nitrogen is all around you, but opening the bond costs more energy than almost any other diatomic.
notes.extra: In practice: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at ~400–500 °C, 150–300 atm, Fe catalyst. Roughly half the nitrogen in your body passed through a Haber plant.

notes.front: Nitrogen is diatomic N₂, but white phosphorus is P₄. Why the difference?
notes.back: P atoms are bigger, so side-on 3p–3p π overlap is poor and P≡P is weak. Six P–P single bonds in a tetrahedron beat two P≡P triples.
notes.extra: Consequence: phosphorus chemistry is single-bond and P–O based (strong P–O ~360 kJ/mol): phosphates in DNA, adenosine triphosphate (ATP), bone and fertiliser.

notes.front: Why does carbon build life's chains while silicon builds rock?
notes.back: Si–Si and Si–H bonds are weak and reactive, but Si–O (~450 kJ/mol) is very strong. Silicon ends up as SiO₂ and silicates, solid networks, not chains.
notes.analogy: Carbon's waste product (CO₂) is a gas you can breathe out; silicon's waste product is sand, which you would have to excrete as rock.
notes.extra: Why silicon life is unlikely: no soluble, gaseous oxide for metabolism, and long silanes burn or hydrolyse on contact with air and water.

notes.front: Why is fluorine the most violent oxidiser, even attacking glass and water?
notes.back: The F–F bond is unusually weak (~158 kJ/mol, lone-pair repulsion on small atoms) while bonds F forms are extremely strong (H–F ~565 kJ/mol). Reactions are very downhill.
notes.extra: Trend: E° (X₂/X⁻) = +2.87 F, +1.36 Cl, +1.07 Br, +0.54 I V. Iodine is the weak oxidiser, which is why iodised salt uses stable iodide or iodate.

notes.front: What is the actual disinfectant in a chlorinated pool, and why does pool pH matter?
notes.back: Hypochlorous acid, HOCl. Its pKa is ~7.5: below, mostly HOCl (potent); above pH 8, mostly OCl⁻, a much weaker disinfectant. Hold pH ~7.2–7.6.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the sharp 'chlorine smell' is chloramines formed when HOCl meets sweat or urine, not free chlorine. It means the pool needs more chlorine, not less.

notes.front: Why does water boil at 100 °C while the heavier H₂S boils near −60 °C?
notes.back: Each H₂O makes up to four hydrogen bonds (~20 kJ/mol each) that must be broken to vaporise. Sulfur is too large and too weakly electronegative to hydrogen-bond.
notes.extra: Also: the same network makes water's heat capacity, surface tension and solvent power unusually high.

notes.front: Why do transition metals show many oxidation states (Mn from +2 to +7)?
notes.back: 4s and 3d energies are close, so removing successive electrons from both sets costs only gradually more energy, and many ions stay stable.
notes.extra: Example: Mn²⁺ (pale pink), MnO₂ (brown), MnO₄⁻ (purple) are the same element in three states.

notes.front: Why are many transition-metal ions coloured, while Zn²⁺ and Sc³⁺ are colourless?
notes.back: Ligands split the d orbitals by an energy in the visible range. The ion absorbs that colour (d–d transition) and shows the complement. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions have no d–d transition.
notes.extra: Example: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs orange-red and looks blue. Intense MnO₄⁻ purple is a different mechanism: ligand-to-metal charge transfer.

notes.front: Why does ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) appear in shampoo and also treat lead poisoning?
notes.back: EDTA is a hexadentate ligand that wraps one metal ion with six donors. In shampoo it grabs Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ and iron; as CaNa₂EDTA it swaps Ca²⁺ for Pb²⁺, which is then excreted.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the sodium-only salt strips blood calcium dangerously; the clinical drug is the calcium form.

notes.front: Why is a chelate like [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ more stable than [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺? Enthalpy or entropy?
notes.back: Mainly entropy. Each bidentate en displaces two NH₃, so 4 particles in become 7 out: free ligands gain disorder, and ΔH is roughly equal.
notes.analogy: Swapping six single paperclips for three linked pairs: many more loose pieces float free.
notes.extra: Why it matters: chelating drugs, water softeners and metal sensors rely on this extra stability, worth many orders of magnitude in K.

notes.front: How does cisplatin kill cancer cells, and why must it be the cis isomer?
notes.back: Square-planar Pt(II) loses chloride inside the cell (low Cl⁻ there) and binds two adjacent guanine N7 atoms on DNA, kinking it. The trans isomer cannot make that crosslink.
notes.extra: In practice: effective for testicular cancer. Geometry, not composition, decides activity: same formula, opposite biology.

notes.front: In octahedral crystal-field splitting, why do high-spin and low-spin d⁶ ions arise?
notes.back: Ligands raise e_g above t₂g by Δₒ. If Δₒ is smaller than the pairing energy P, electrons spread out (high spin); if larger, they pair in t₂g (low spin).
notes.analogy: Do people take separate seats (cost: climbing to the upper deck) or share a seat (cost: pairing repulsion)? Whichever is cheaper wins.
notes.extra: Pattern: only d⁴–d⁷ have a choice. 4d/5d metals are almost always low spin.

notes.front: Why are ruby and emerald red and green when both owe their colour to Cr³⁺?
notes.back: Same ion, different host. In corundum (ruby) Cr–O distances are short, giving larger Δₒ and absorption of yellow-green; in beryl (emerald) Δₒ is smaller and red is absorbed.
notes.extra: Bonus: ruby also fluoresces red, which is how the first laser worked.

notes.text: Spectrochemical series (weak to strong field): I⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < {{c1::H₂O}} < {{c2::NH₃}} < en < {{c3::CN⁻}} ≈ {{c4::CO}}. Strong-field ligands give {{c5::large}} Δₒ.
notes.extra: Also: Δ increases with metal oxidation state and down a group (3d < 4d < 5d).

notes.front: Crystal field vs ligand field theory: what does the second add?
notes.back: Crystal field treats ligands as point charges; ligand field uses molecular orbitals, adding covalency and π-bonding. That explains why neutral CO sits above F⁻ in the series.
notes.extra: Limit of CFT: a pure electrostatic model should rank OH⁻ above H₂O; it fails because π-donor and π-acceptor effects dominate.

notes.front: Why does the 18-electron rule predict stable organometallics like ferrocene, and how do catalysts use 16e complexes?
notes.back: A metal has nine valence orbitals (s, 3×p, 5×d), filled by 18 electrons. Fe(C₅H₅)₂ = 8 + 2×5 = 18. 16e complexes (Wilkinson's, Grubbs) add a substrate, reach 18e, react and regenerate.
notes.extra: Examples: Wilkinson's RhCl(PPh₃)₃ hydrogenates alkenes; Grubbs' Ru carbene swaps alkene partners (metathesis).

notes.front: What does HSAB predict, and why does mercury bind sulfur so strongly?
notes.back: Hard acids prefer hard bases (Ca²⁺ with O, F⁻); soft acids prefer soft bases. Hg²⁺ is large and polarisable, so it bonds covalently to soft sulfur (cysteine –SH).
notes.analogy: Like plugs and sockets: matching polarisability fits.
notes.extra: In practice: Hg and Cd poison enzymes by binding thiols; thiol chelators (dimercaprol) are antidotes.

notes.front: Why does cyanide let a gold mine extract gold from rock when plain air cannot?
notes.back: Soft Au⁺ binds CN⁻ so strongly that Au⁺/Au drops from +1.69 V to about −0.60 V as [Au(CN)₂]⁻, so dissolved O₂ can oxidise gold.
notes.extra: In practice: 4Au + 8CN⁻ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + 4OH⁻; gold is then recovered on carbon or zinc. Toxicity and spills are the cost.

notes.front: Why do NaCl and CsCl crystallise in different structures?
notes.back: Radius ratio. Na⁺/Cl⁻ ≈ 0.52 fits six anions (octahedral); Cs⁺/Cl⁻ ≈ 0.93 is big enough for eight (cubic). Cations touch anions but anions must not touch each other.
notes.analogy: Packing oranges around a grapefruit versus around a marble.
notes.extra: Background: close-packed spheres fill 74% of space, with 12 neighbours; ionic salts are close-packed anions with cations in holes.

notes.front: How does doping make n-type and p-type silicon?
notes.back: Add phosphorus (5 valence electrons) for a free electron: n-type. Add boron (3) for a missing electron, a hole: p-type. A few ppm raises conductivity enormously.
notes.analogy: Slip one extra tenant into a full building (n) or take away a chair (p): in both cases something can now move.
notes.extra: Defects matter: the same idea in ionic solids, where vacancies, Frenkel and Schottky defects let ions hop and tint crystals.

notes.front: Why are perovskites such as CH₃NH₃PbI₃ exciting for solar cells?
notes.back: ABX₃ crystals absorb sunlight strongly at a band gap near 1.5 eV (tunable by changing the halide) and tolerate defects, so thin cheap solution-processed films give high efficiency.
notes.extra: Problems: lead toxicity and degradation by moisture and heat, so stability, not efficiency, is the bottleneck.

notes.front: What makes zeolites useful as molecular sieves?
notes.back: They are aluminosilicate frameworks with uniform pores 0.3–1 nm wide. Only molecules small enough enter, and the charged framework holds polar guests tightly.
notes.analogy: A bouncer with a measuring tape at the door.
notes.extra: Uses: drying solvents (3A/4A), detergent water-softening by Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange, cracking petroleum (ZSM-5), cat litter.

notes.front: Is the setting of cement drying? What is the chemistry?
notes.back: No. Calcium silicates react with water (hydration) to form a calcium silicate hydrate gel plus Ca(OH)₂. The gel interlocks and hardens, even under water.
notes.analogy: Like epoxy curing rather than paint drying: it reacts, it does not just lose solvent.
notes.extra: Why rebar survives: Ca(OH)₂ keeps concrete alkaline (pH ~13), passivating steel. CO₂ slowly neutralises it, and the rust starts.

notes.front: Why are neodymium (NdFeB) magnets so strong, and where do you find them?
notes.back: Nd³⁺ has several unpaired, tightly bound 4f electrons giving a large anisotropic magnetic moment, locked in place by the crystal lattice with iron's strong magnetisation.
notes.extra: In practice: phone speakers and vibration motors, hard drives, EV and wind-turbine motors. Eu³⁺ and Tb³⁺ make red and green screen phosphors.

notes.front: How can you spot a species that will disproportionate on a Frost diagram?
notes.back: A Frost diagram plots nE° against oxidation state. A species lying above the straight line joining its neighbours is unstable and splits into them (e.g. Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺).
notes.analogy: A ball on a hilltop between two valleys: it rolls to one side or the other.
notes.extra: Reading it: slope between points = E° of that couple. Latimer diagrams list the same E° values on arrows between oxidation states.

notes.front: What is an orbital really, and what do the textbook pictures show?
notes.back: An orbital is a one-electron wavefunction ψ. Its square |ψ|² is probability density; the picture is a surface enclosing ~90% of that probability. Colours mark phase (sign), not charge.
notes.analogy: A heat-map of where a bird is likely to be found, not a flight path.
notes.extra: Pitfall: an electron does not orbit in that shape; there is no trajectory to draw.

notes.front: How many radial and angular nodes does an orbital with quantum numbers n and ℓ have?
notes.back: Radial nodes = n − ℓ − 1; angular nodes = ℓ; total n − 1. So 2s has one spherical node, 2p has one planar node and no radial node.
notes.extra: Why care: nodes mean zero electron density; they set energy and phase patterns that govern bonding.

notes.front: Why does 4s fill before 3d, yet 4s electrons leave first when a transition metal ionises?
notes.back: In K and Ca, 4s penetrates close to the nucleus and is lower in energy. Once 3d electrons are present, the nucleus pulls 3d lower, so 4s is the outer, higher electron to leave.
notes.extra: Check: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶, not [Ar]3d⁴4s².

notes.front: How do orbital shapes explain molecular geometry such as water's 104.5° angle?
notes.back: Bonds form by overlap along lobes. Pure p orbitals would give 90°; mixing in s character (hybridisation) and lone-pair repulsion open the angle toward tetrahedral.
notes.extra: Pitfall: hybridisation is a bookkeeping device for geometry, not a physical event. H₂S at 92° is nearly pure p.

notes.front: What does the Born–Oppenheimer approximation license chemists to say?
notes.back: Nuclei are ~1800× heavier than electrons, so freeze them, solve the electrons, and get an energy as a function of geometry. That gives a molecular structure and a potential energy surface.
notes.analogy: Solving a game's physics for the player while the map is paused, then moving the map one step.
notes.extra: Where it fails: conical intersections in photochemistry and fast light-atom motion.

notes.front: In linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO), how do bonding and antibonding orbitals arise, and why is He₂ not a molecule?
notes.back: Adding two atomic orbitals in phase builds density between nuclei (bonding, lower energy); out of phase leaves a node between them (antibonding, higher). He₂ fills both, giving bond order zero.
notes.analogy: Two waves in phase add up; out of phase they cancel in the middle.
notes.extra: Formula: bond order = ½(bonding − antibonding electrons).

notes.front: Why does a longer conjugated π system absorb at longer wavelength (more red)?
notes.back: In Hückel theory, π orbitals spread over more atoms, so the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO)–lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) gap shrinks. A smaller gap means lower-energy light is absorbed.
notes.analogy: A longer guitar string vibrates at a lower pitch.
notes.extra: Examples: ethene absorbs in the UV; β-carotene (11 conjugated C=C) absorbs blue and looks orange; retinal in vision.

notes.front: What is the variational principle and why does every computational method rely on it?
notes.back: Any trial wavefunction gives an energy ≥ the true ground-state energy. So you improve a guess by lowering its energy, and the lowest one is the best.
notes.extra: Used in: Hartree–Fock, basis-set expansions, and variational parameters in post-HF methods.

notes.front: What does Hartree–Fock assume, and what does it miss?
notes.back: Each electron moves in the average field of the others (mean field) using a single Slater determinant. It includes exchange but not instantaneous electron–electron avoidance (correlation).
notes.analogy: Judging traffic by average density rather than by each car's reaction to the car beside it.
notes.extra: In practice: Hartree–Fock (HF) recovers ~99% of total energy but chemistry lives in the remaining 1%; it describes bond breaking poorly.

notes.front: What is electron correlation, and which everyday force is purely a correlation effect?
notes.back: Correlation is electrons dodging each other instantaneously, beyond mean-field. Correlation energy = exact minus Hartree–Fock (HF) energy. London dispersion forces arise from it.
notes.extra: Example: HF predicts no attraction between two argon atoms; correlated methods and real argon liquefy.

notes.front: What does MP2 do, and when is it a sensible choice?
notes.back: Second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation theory adds a correction for pairwise electron correlation on top of Hartree–Fock (HF) at ~N⁵ cost. Good value for dispersion and moderate-size molecules.
notes.extra: Limits: overbinds π-stacked systems and fails for near-degenerate or metallic systems.

notes.front: Why is coupled cluster singles, doubles and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)) called the 'gold standard' of quantum chemistry?
notes.back: Coupled cluster with singles, doubles and perturbative triples gets small-molecule energies within ~1 kcal/mol (chemical accuracy), but costs ~N⁷, so it is limited to dozens of atoms.
notes.extra: In practice: used to benchmark density functional theory (DFT) functionals and train machine-learned potentials.

notes.front: What is the Hohenberg–Kohn idea behind density functional theory (DFT)?
notes.back: The ground-state energy is a functional of the electron density ρ(r), a function of 3 variables, not the wavefunction of 3N variables. Kohn–Sham hides the unknown part in the exchange–correlation functional.
notes.extra: Catch: the exact functional is unknown, so all practical DFT is approximate.

notes.front: Why does density functional theory (DFT; B3LYP) dominate everyday computational chemistry?
notes.back: Accuracy near correlated methods at ~N³–N⁴ cost, so hundreds of atoms are feasible. B3LYP is a hybrid: it mixes ~20% exact Hartree–Fock (HF) exchange into a gradient-corrected functional.
notes.extra: Reality: functional choice is empirical; validate against experiment or coupled cluster singles, doubles and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)).

notes.text: Standard density functional theory (DFT) struggles with {{c1::dispersion (London) forces}}, {{c2::self-interaction error}} (electrons repelling themselves), and {{c3::strongly correlated}} systems such as stretched bonds and some metal clusters.
notes.extra: Fix: add empirical dispersion corrections (D3/D4); use multireference methods for strong correlation.

notes.front: What does the basis set 6-31G* mean in words?
notes.back: Each core orbital is one function built from 6 Gaussians; each valence orbital is split into two functions (3 and 1 Gaussians); * adds d polarisation functions on heavy atoms.
notes.analogy: Choosing pixel resolution: more functions, sharper picture, higher cost.
notes.extra: Add-ons: '+' means diffuse functions, needed for anions and weak interactions.

notes.front: What is a transition state on a potential energy surface, and how is it recognised computationally?
notes.back: A first-order saddle point: a maximum along the reaction coordinate, a minimum in all other directions. It shows exactly one imaginary vibrational frequency.
notes.analogy: The mountain pass between two valleys: highest point on the easiest path.
notes.extra: In practice: follow the intrinsic reaction coordinate downhill to verify it links the intended reactant and product.

notes.front: What does a protein-folding simulation actually compute?
notes.back: A force field treats atoms as balls and springs plus Coulomb and van der Waals terms; Newton's laws advance positions every ~2 fs. No electrons, and bonds do not break.
notes.analogy: A physics-engine game running millions of tiny frames.
notes.extra: Limits: folding takes microseconds to seconds, so enhanced sampling or special hardware is needed.

notes.front: Why is CO₂ a greenhouse gas but N₂ is not?
notes.back: A vibration absorbs infrared only if the dipole changes. CO₂'s bend and asymmetric stretch do (a quantised photon matches the energy gap); N₂'s lone stretch is symmetric, so no dipole change.
notes.extra: Key band: CO₂'s bend near 15 µm absorbs Earth's outgoing thermal radiation. O₂ and N₂ are transparent.

notes.front: Is a microwave oven tuned to a resonance of water?
notes.back: No. 2.45 GHz is a regulatory band with convenient penetration depth. Liquid water absorbs broadly by dielectric friction as molecules try to rotate with the oscillating field.
notes.extra: Evidence: ice barely absorbs, so frozen food heats unevenly. Free-water rotational lines are at much higher frequencies.

notes.front: Fluorescence vs phosphorescence: how do they differ and why is one a 'glow-in-the-dark'?
notes.back: Fluorescence is S₁→S₀ emission, spin-allowed, over nanoseconds. Phosphorescence is T₁→S₀, spin-forbidden after intersystem crossing, lasting milliseconds to hours.
notes.analogy: Fluorescence is a light switch; phosphorescence is a capacitor slowly discharging through a forbidden path.
notes.extra: Also: emission is redder than absorption (Stokes shift) because energy is lost to vibrations first.

notes.front: What does the Franck–Condon principle say about electronic transitions?
notes.back: Electrons jump in ~10⁻¹⁵ s, far faster than nuclei move, so transitions are vertical on the potential-energy plot; the overlap of vibrational wavefunctions sets which vibrational peaks are strong.
notes.extra: Result: the vibrational fine structure and the mirror-image shape of absorption and fluorescence bands.

notes.front: What is nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) from the quantum angle?
notes.back: Nuclei with spin ½ (¹H, ¹³C) in a magnetic field split into two energy levels; radio waves flip them. Local electrons shield the field, giving each environment a different chemical shift.
notes.extra: Same physics: MRI images the NMR signal of water protons. Signals are weak, as the population difference is only ~1 in 10⁵.

notes.front: What is the Jahn–Teller effect and where do you see it in Cu²⁺ complexes?
notes.back: A non-linear molecule in an electronically degenerate state distorts to lift the degeneracy. High-spin d⁴ and d⁹ (Cu²⁺) octahedral complexes show two long and four short bonds.
notes.analogy: A table with a leg of different length: the symmetric arrangement is unstable, so it settles lopsided.
notes.extra: In practice: why Cu²⁺ complexes are rarely perfectly octahedral and why they are so strongly coloured.

notes.front: Why does quantum tunnelling matter for hydrogen transfer in enzymes?
notes.back: Light particles pass through a barrier instead of climbing over it. H tunnels more than D, so replacing H with D can slow a reaction by far more than the classical maximum of ~7.
notes.extra: Example: soybean lipoxygenase has a kinetic isotope effect near 80, evidence of tunnelling.

notes.front: How do machine-learned potentials and AlphaFold-style tools change computational chemistry?
notes.back: Neural networks trained on density functional theory (DFT) or coupled cluster singles, doubles and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)) energies give near-quantum accuracy at near-force-field speed. AlphaFold predicts structure from sequence by learned patterns, not by simulating folding.
notes.extra: Caveat: they fail outside the training distribution, and they do not explain the underlying physics.

notes.text: Each macromolecule is joined by its own bond: proteins by the {{c1::amide (peptide)}} bond, DNA by the {{c2::phosphodiester}} bond, carbohydrates by the {{c3::glycosidic}} bond, fats (triglycerides) by the {{c4::ester}} bond.
notes.extra: Common trick: all four are made by condensation (lose H₂O) and broken by hydrolysis (add H₂O). Digestion is hydrolysis; enzymes make it fast.

notes.front: Why does the side chain of an amino acid decide a protein's behaviour?
notes.back: The backbone is identical in all 20; only the side chain differs (charged, polar, hydrophobic, special). It sets where each residue sits in the folded protein and what it can bind or catalyse.
notes.analogy: The 20 side chains are the 20 keys on a keyboard; the backbone is just the identical chassis every key sits on.

notes.front: Why is the peptide bond flat and rigid?
notes.back: The N lone pair delocalises into C=O, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character. Rotation is restricted, so only the bonds either side (φ, ψ) twist.
notes.extra: Consequence: backbone shape is set by two angles per residue, which is what makes helices and sheets possible.

notes.front: What drives a protein to fold into a compact shape?
notes.back: Hydrophobic collapse: water prefers hydrogen-bonding to itself, so oily side chains bury in the core. Hydrogen bonds (helices, sheets) and salt bridges then lock the shape.
notes.analogy: Like oil droplets merging in a salad dressing: the driver is the water's freedom, not the oil's attraction.
notes.extra: Why: burying hydrophobic groups frees ordered water molecules, so entropy rises.

notes.front: Why does egg white turn white and solid when cooked, and why is high fever dangerous?
notes.back: Heat breaks the weak bonds holding the fold. Unfolded proteins expose hydrophobic cores, stick together and scatter light. Body proteins start to denature a few degrees above normal.
notes.extra: Irreversible: cooking an egg does not unboil it; the tangled aggregate is a deeper trap than the folded state. Acid and alcohol also denature.

notes.front: Lock-and-key vs induced fit: what is the difference?
notes.back: Lock-and-key: the active site is a rigid, ready-made match for the substrate. Induced fit: the site reshapes as the substrate binds, and fits best to the transition state.
notes.analogy: A rigid mould versus a glove that closes around the hand and squeezes it into a particular pose.

notes.front: Why are enzymes up to \(10^{17}\) times faster than the uncatalysed reaction?
notes.back: They bind the transition state more tightly than the substrate, lowering the activation barrier. They also orient reactants and supply acid, base or metal groups exactly where needed.
notes.extra: Pitfall: an enzyme changes the rate, not the equilibrium or ΔG of the reaction.

notes.front: What are cofactors, and how do vitamins relate to them?
notes.back: Cofactors are non-protein helpers (metal ions, or organic coenzymes). Many B vitamins are precursors of coenzymes such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and coenzyme A (CoA), which is why a deficiency stalls metabolism.
notes.analogy: The enzyme is the machine; the coenzyme is the swappable tool head that the machine cannot make itself.

notes.text: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis releases about {{c1::30 kJ/mol}} under standard biochemical conditions, because its phosphate {{c2::anhydride}} bonds are strained by crowded negative charges and the products are better stabilised.
notes.extra: Not a high-energy bond: the energy comes from the whole reaction (charge relief, resonance of Pᵢ, solvation), not from the bond itself.

notes.front: How does adenosine triphosphate (ATP) make an uphill reaction go?
notes.back: Coupling: the enzyme links the uphill step to ATP hydrolysis (often via a phosphorylated intermediate). The summed ΔG is negative, so the pair proceeds.
notes.analogy: A pump with a flywheel: you cannot lift water uphill for free, but you can if the same shaft drops a heavier weight.

notes.front: What do nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺/NADH) do in metabolism?
notes.back: They shuttle electrons (as hydride, H⁻). Oxidising food reduces NAD⁺ to NADH; NADH delivers its electrons to the respiratory chain, where they end up on oxygen.
notes.analogy: Reusable batteries or courier vans: loaded at the oxidation steps, unloaded at the power plant.

notes.front: Why is oxygen the final electron acceptor, and why does cyanide kill?
notes.back: O₂ has a very high reduction potential, so electrons falling onto it release the most energy. Cyanide binds the iron of cytochrome c oxidase, blocking the last step; the chain backs up and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) stops.
notes.extra: Same logic: carbon monoxide and azide also hit this enzyme or haemoglobin's iron.

notes.front: Why doesn't the body burn glucose like a flame, though the net reaction is the same?
notes.back: Combustion would dump about 2800 kJ/mol as heat at once. Cells oxidise glucose in about 30 enzyme-controlled steps and capture roughly a third of the energy as adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
notes.analogy: Instead of one dam collapse, a staircase of small water wheels, each turning a generator.

notes.front: Why does fat store about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate (~37 vs ~17 kJ/g)?
notes.back: Fat's carbons are more reduced: mostly C–H bonds, little oxygen. More electrons are available to be given to O₂ per gram, and fat is stored without water.
notes.extra: Hydrogen count: think of fat as 'already half-fuel', whereas sugar is partly oxidised already.

notes.front: How is the DNA double helix held together, and why do guanine–cytosine (GC)-rich stretches melt at a higher temperature?
notes.back: Base-pair hydrogen bonds (A–T two, G–C three) give specificity; base stacking gives most of the stability. G–C has more H-bonds and stacks better, so it needs more heat to separate.
notes.extra: In practice: primers in polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are designed with a target melting temperature, which depends on GC content.

notes.front: How does polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplify DNA using only chemistry?
notes.back: Repeat three steps: heat (about 95 °C) separates strands, cool lets primers anneal, then a heat-stable polymerase (about 72 °C) extends them. Each cycle doubles the copies.
notes.analogy: A photocopier whose output is fed back as input: 30 cycles give about a billion copies.
notes.extra: Why Taq: from a hot-spring bacterium; it survives the 95 °C steps.

notes.front: Why do phospholipids spontaneously form a bilayer, by the same principle as soap?
notes.back: A polar head loves water, two oily tails hate it. In water the tails hide inward and heads face out, forming sheets that close into vesicles. Cholesterol tucks in to tune fluidity.
notes.extra: Same as soap: a micelle is a one-tail version; no covalent bonds are needed, just hydrophobic effect.

notes.front: How do hormones and receptors work chemically?
notes.back: Molecular recognition: the hormone's shape and charges fit a receptor pocket through many weak interactions. Binding changes the receptor's shape, starting a signal. Peptide hormones act at the cell surface, steroids inside.
notes.analogy: A key that does not open the door but flips a switch on it.

notes.front: Why is ibuprofen an acid, and how does pKa govern its absorption?
notes.back: Its carboxylic acid (pKa about 4.4) is mostly neutral in stomach acid, so it crosses membranes. In blood (pH 7.4) it ionises, dissolving well while the COO⁻ group binds the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme.
notes.extra: Why most drugs are small: oral drugs tend to be below about 500 Da (Lipinski's rules), so they can cross gut membranes.

notes.front: Addition vs condensation polymerisation: how do polyethylene and nylon differ in making?
notes.back: Addition: monomers with C=C open and add to a chain, nothing lost (polyethylene). Condensation: two functional groups join and release a small molecule, e.g. H₂O, as in nylon's amide links.
notes.analogy: Addition is clipping carriages onto a train; condensation is coupling them with a bolt that drops a washer each time.

notes.front: Why is a polymer glassy in a freezer but rubbery at room temperature?
notes.back: Below its glass transition temperature (Tg) the chains are frozen in place and brittle; above it segments wriggle and the material is soft. Crystalline regions stiffen it further.
notes.analogy: Cold honey versus warm honey; same molecules, but the chains can slide past one another or not.
notes.extra: In practice: rubber hoses crack in deep cold; polyethylene terephthalate (PET) bottles are glassy at room temperature (Tg about 70 °C).

notes.front: How does vulcanisation turn sticky rubber into tyre rubber?
notes.back: Sulfur forms cross-links between chains, so they can stretch but spring back instead of flowing. More sulfur gives a harder, less elastic rubber.
notes.analogy: Individual strands of spaghetti are runny; spaghetti stitched together at points is a net that springs back.

notes.front: How does the backbone and side group explain polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)?
notes.back: PET: ester links in a stiff aromatic chain, strong and clear. PVC: polar C–Cl groups stick chains together, stiff unless plasticised. PTFE: a sheath of strong C–F bonds, so inert, slippery and heat-resistant.

notes.front: Thermoplastic vs thermoset: what is the key difference and why does it matter?
notes.back: Thermoplastics are separate chains that soften when heated, so they can be remelted and recycled. Thermosets are covalently cross-linked in a network and char instead, so they cannot be remelted.
notes.analogy: Wax candle versus baked cake: warm one softens again, the other only burns.
notes.extra: Examples: polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), both thermoplastic; epoxy resin, Bakelite (thermoset).

notes.front: Why do most plastics persist for centuries, and why does polylactic acid (PLA) not?
notes.back: Carbon–carbon backbones have no weak link microbes can hydrolyse. PLA is a polyester: water and enzymes (at industrial composting heat) break its ester links back into lactic acid.
notes.extra: Recycling logic: chemically recycle condensation polymers (such as polyethylene terephthalate, PET) by reversing their formation (depolymerisation).

notes.front: Why are silicones and Kevlar so different in character from polyethylene?
notes.back: Silicones have a Si–O backbone: flexible, heat-stable, water-repellent. Kevlar has stiff aromatic rings with amide groups that line up and hydrogen-bond between chains, giving steel-like strength.
notes.analogy: Silicone is a limber chain of ball joints; Kevlar is a bundle of rods velcroed to each other side to side.

notes.front: Accuracy vs precision: what is the difference?
notes.back: Accuracy: closeness to the true value (small bias). Precision: closeness of repeats to each other (small scatter). You can be precise yet wrong.
notes.analogy: A load-balancer that always sends traffic to the same wrong server: perfectly consistent, perfectly incorrect.
notes.extra: Fix: calibrate against a standard to cure bias; average repeats to improve precision.

notes.front: How does a calibration curve turn a signal into a concentration?
notes.back: Measure standards of known concentration, fit signal versus concentration, then read the unknown off the line. Keep the unknown inside the range of the standards.
notes.extra: Limit of detection (LOD): about 3 × blank noise ÷ slope. Errors live in sample prep (contamination, losses), not the instrument.

notes.front: What is the logic of a titration?
notes.back: Add a reagent of exact concentration until the reaction is stoichiometrically complete (equivalence point), then calculate the unknown from moles = concentration × volume.
notes.extra: Endpoint vs equivalence: the indicator colour change (endpoint) should land at the true equivalence point.

notes.front: Reading this titration curve: why does the choice of indicator depend on the equivalence pH?
notes.back: Weak acid + strong base ends above pH 7 (the conjugate base is basic). Phenolphthalein changes at 8.2–10, matching the steep jump; methyl orange (3–4.5) would change far too early.
notes.extra: Half-equivalence: pH = pKa, so the curve also measures the acid's pKa.

notes.front: How does chromatography separate compounds?
notes.back: A mobile phase carries the mixture over a stationary phase. Compounds partition differently between them: those that stick more lag, those that dissolve in the mobile phase run ahead.
notes.analogy: A river with sticky reeds: light swimmers who cling to the bank arrive later than those who stay in the current.
notes.extra: Variants: thin-layer chromatography (TLC), gas chromatography (GC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Drug tests use liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS): mass adds a second identity check beyond retention time.

notes.text: The {{c1::Beer–Lambert}} law says absorbance \(A = \varepsilon l c\) is proportional to {{c2::concentration}}, so a colourimeter measures how much dye is in a solution.
notes.extra: Limit: it fails at high concentration (curved calibration), so dilute until A is below about 1.

notes.front: Atomic absorption vs inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) for lead in drinking water: what is the difference?
notes.back: AAS: lead atoms in a flame absorb a lamp's lead-specific light, measuring one element at a time. ICP-MS: a 6000+ K plasma ionises everything and a mass spectrometer counts ions, reaching parts per trillion.
notes.analogy: AAS is a single-purpose metal detector; ICP-MS is a full inventory scan.

notes.front: How do a glucose meter and a breathalyser sense chemistry?
notes.back: Glucose strip: glucose oxidase makes electrons, and the current is proportional to glucose. Breathalyser fuel cell: ethanol is oxidised at a platinum electrode, and the current is proportional to alcohol.
notes.extra: Shared principle: a redox reaction turns concentration into a measurable current.

notes.front: Why do flame tests give colours, and how does this relate to fireworks?
notes.back: Heat excites electrons; falling back they emit light of a line-specific wavelength. Sodium glows yellow, strontium red, barium green, copper blue.
notes.extra: Fireworks: metal salts supply the colour, oxidiser and fuel supply the heat; blue is hardest because copper chloride decomposes if too hot.

notes.front: How does a lateral-flow pregnancy test work, and how does an antigen test differ from polymerase chain reaction (PCR)?
notes.back: Antibodies on the strip capture human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), bound to dye-labelled antibodies, forming a line. Antigen tests detect viral protein this way; PCR amplifies viral genetic material, so it is far more sensitive.
notes.analogy: Antigen test is a quick ID check at the door; PCR photocopies the faintest trace until it is obvious.

notes.front: Ozone layer vs ozone smog: why is one good and one bad?
notes.back: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV, protecting life. Ground-level ozone forms from NOₓ and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) under sunlight and damages lungs. Same molecule, different altitude and role.
notes.extra: Cause of the hole: chlorine from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) catalytically destroys ozone, one Cl atom destroying thousands of O₃.

notes.front: Why do CO₂, CH₄ and water vapour trap heat but N₂ and O₂ do not?
notes.back: Their vibrations change the molecule's dipole, so they absorb infrared. Symmetric diatomics like N₂ and O₂ have no dipole change and are IR-transparent.
notes.analogy: A sunroom roof that lets light in but is opaque to the infrared that tries to leave.

notes.front: What causes hard water, and how does it scale a kettle?
notes.back: Dissolved Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ (with HCO₃⁻). Heating drives off CO₂ and precipitates CaCO₃ as limescale. Softeners use ion exchange, swapping Ca²⁺ for Na⁺.
notes.extra: Soap scum: Ca²⁺ also precipitates soap, which is why hard water lathers poorly.

notes.front: What are the main steps in water treatment, and why chlorine or ozone?
notes.back: Alum coagulates fine particles into floc that settles; filtration removes the rest; then a disinfectant. Chlorine leaves a lasting residue, while ozone is stronger but vanishes.
notes.extra: Fluoride: added to harden tooth enamel (fluorapatite).

notes.front: Why are per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) called 'forever chemicals'?
notes.back: The C–F bond is among the strongest in organic chemistry, and the fluorine shield protects the carbon chain. Nature has few enzymes or conditions that break it.
notes.extra: Why useful: they repel both water and oil, which is why they sit in non-stick pans and waterproofing.

notes.front: Why does lead stay toxic for years after exposure?
notes.back: Pb²⁺ mimics Ca²⁺ and replaces it in bone mineral, a slow-release reservoir. As a soft acid it also binds enzyme thiols and blocks haem synthesis.
notes.extra: Treatment: chelators with soft donor atoms (e.g. dimercaprol) grab the metal.

notes.front: How does amine scrubbing capture CO₂, and what is the alternative?
notes.back: A basic amine solution reacts with CO₂ to bind it at about 40 °C; heating to about 120 °C releases pure CO₂ for storage. Mineralisation instead converts CO₂ into solid carbonate rock.
notes.analogy: A sponge that soaks when cool and is squeezed when hot.

notes.text: The Contact process makes {{c1::sulfuric acid}} with a {{c2::V₂O₅}} catalyst, and chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine gives {{c3::Cl₂, NaOH and H₂}}.
notes.extra: Why they matter: sulfuric acid use is a classic index of industrial activity; NaOH and Cl₂ feed soap, paper, polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and bleach.

notes.front: What do cracking and reforming do to crude oil fractions?
notes.back: Cracking breaks long, low-value alkanes into short alkenes and petrol-range molecules. Reforming rearranges them into branched or aromatic molecules with higher octane.
notes.analogy: Cracking is breaking logs into kindling; reforming is re-stacking them into a form that burns evenly.

notes.front: Why does making cement release so much CO₂?
notes.back: Limestone is heated: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, so the raw material itself releases CO₂ on top of the fuel burned. About 60% of cement CO₂ comes from the limestone.
notes.extra: Solvay process: similarly turns limestone and brine into soda ash (Na₂CO₃) for glass.

notes.front: Atom economy vs E-factor: what does each measure?
notes.back: Atom economy: the fraction of reactant atoms ending up in the product (theoretical). E-factor: kg of waste per kg of product (real, including solvents).
notes.extra: E-factor: bulk chemicals 1–5, pharma 25–100+ (many steps, high purity). Flow reactors cut waste and risk.

notes.front: Why are nitrogen-rich compounds such as trinitrotoluene (TNT) and nitroglycerin explosive?
notes.back: They hold weak N–N or N–O bonds and decompose to N₂, whose triple bond is extremely strong. The huge energy released and the sudden gas expansion produce the blast.
notes.analogy: A boulder balanced on a hilltop: a small push sends it into a very deep valley.

notes.front: How do cleaning chemistries work: surfactants, bleach, enzymes, hot water?
notes.back: Surfactants lift oil into micelles; bleach oxidises coloured stains; enzymes cut protein and starch; heat lowers viscosity and speeds dissolution and reaction.
notes.extra: Never mix: bleach with ammonia or acid releases toxic chloramines or chlorine gas.

notes.front: Baking soda vs baking powder: what is the difference?
notes.back: Baking soda is NaHCO₃ and needs an acid in the batter to release CO₂. Baking powder is soda plus a dry acid, so it only needs moisture and heat.
notes.extra: Salt in pasta water: adds flavour, but barely changes boiling point (about 0.5 °C for a spoonful in a pot).
